______________________________________________________________________

## 4. Troubleshooting

| Symptom                                                                                        | Cause and fix                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Camera log: *Waiting for simulator at …:53335 (World not running?)*                            | Isaac Sim is not playing, the camera host is wrong, or a firewall blocks port 53335                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| Camera log: *…publishes frames of camera(s) … but none of camera 'cam0'*                       | **Camera name** does not match a camera in the scene                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| Camera log: *Frames … are stale or carry capture times that do not match this Station's clock* | The clocks of the two computers differ. Synchronize them (NTP), or stop sending capture times at the source (Isaac Sim: start it with `RC_CAMERA_CAPTURE_TIME=0`; Device Bridge: `send_capture_time: false`) so that the Station uses arrival times.                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| Camera image is visible, but the Localizer remains Initializing, Relocalizing or Lost          | Check **horizontal fov deg** against the source camera. A new gateway defaults to 60°, while the Jackal warehouse example uses 90°. Incorrect intrinsics distort the depth points used to match the map, even when the image looks normal. Follow the [settings correction procedure](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/navigation/simulation_tutorial/#correct-settings-on-a-running-setup), then check the initial pose if needed. |
| Camera view is black or frozen                                                                 | The camera prim looks at nothing, or the scene is paused                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |

# Device Bridge

Stellar X connects to the rest of the robot through network ports only. Sensors that need USB, such as an Intel RealSense depth camera or a USB IMU, therefore go on a small computer next to them: a Raspberry Pi, another single-board computer or a PC. The **Device Bridge** runs on that computer. It reads the devices and serves their data to the controller over the LAN.

The bridge speaks the same network protocol as Isaac Bridge, so the controller's built-in Camera gateway, IMU gateway, Visual odometry, Localizer and Navigator connect to real sensors the same way as to a simulated robot: they connect to the sensor computer instead of the Isaac Sim computer. Real sensors still need their own values: camera intrinsics, mounting and synchronized clocks.

Use the Device Bridge when:

- the robot carries a USB camera or IMU, which cannot plug into the controller;
- the motor board of a small robot sits on USB as well (for example the TurtleBot3 OpenCR board) and the controller should drive it.

Drives on the controller's EtherCAT port do not need the bridge, and neither does a simulated robot.

| You want to                                                             | Page                                                                                                         |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Install the bridge, configure its devices and connect it to the Station | This page                                                                                                    |
| Add a driver for your own camera, IMU or wheel board                    | [Write Device Bridge Drivers](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/extend/device_bridge_drivers/index.md) |

The Device Bridge is an open-source program that works with any RGB-D camera, IMU or wheel board through drivers. It comes with example drivers for Intel RealSense D400 cameras, the TurtleBot3 OpenCR board and simulated devices ([Built-in Drivers](#4-built-in-drivers)); other devices connect through a driver that you add. Nothing changes on the controller when you install the bridge or add a driver.

______________________________________________________________________

## 1. Architecture

```
flowchart TB
    subgraph SC ["Sensor computer"]
        DB(["Device Bridge"])
        RS["RealSense<br>depth camera"] --> DB
        IU["USB IMU"] --> DB
        MB["Motor board<br>(optional)"] <--> DB
    end
    subgraph SX ["Stellar X · Stellar Station"]
        CG["Camera gateway"]
        IG["IMU gateway"]
        AG["Actuator gateway<br>(optional)"]
        VO["Visual odometry"]
        LO["Localizer"]
        NV["Navigator"]
        ST["Strider"]
    end
    DB -->|"53335 · RGB-D frames"| CG
    DB -->|"53334 · IMU samples"| IG
    DB <-->|"53333 commands · 53334 joint states"| AG
    CG --> VO
    IG --> VO
    CG --> LO
    VO -->|odometry| LO
    LO -->|"localization · map"| NV
    NV -->|mobile_base| ST
    AG <-->|servo_link| ST
```

The bridge **listens** on three ports and the controller's gateways **connect** to it, exactly as they connect to the simulator. Every message carries the bridge's `robot_name`, and each gateway takes the data published under the name it is configured with. Without the optional wheel stream, Strider drives the robot's own base through an EtherCAT Actuator gateway as usual.

______________________________________________________________________

## 2. Requirements

| Item              | Requirement                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Sensor computer   | A Raspberry Pi, another single-board computer or a PC next to the sensors, running 64-bit Linux with systemd (for example Debian 12, Raspberry Pi OS or Ubuntu). A RealSense camera needs a USB 3 port.                                                                                           |
| Python            | Python 3.8 or later. The installer creates its own environment; when the system Python cannot load the RealSense SDK (for example Debian 12 on 64-bit ARM), it installs a standalone Python 3.10 by itself.                                                                                       |
| Internet          | During installation only, to download the Python packages                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| Network           | The sensor computer and Stellar X on the same LAN; a wired link is recommended                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| Clocks            | Synchronized to within about 20 ms while frames carry their capture time (the default)                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| Firewall          | Inbound TCP ports 53333–53335 on the sensor computer open to the controller                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| Simulator address | Only for an IMU stream: the IMU gateway has no address field and connects to the simulator address set for the controller, which must be the sensor computer ([Addresses Set for the Controller](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/gateways/simulation/#addresses-set-for-the-controller)). |

**Bandwidth.** RGB-D frames travel uncompressed: about 61 Mbit/s at 424 × 240 and 15 fps, about 185 Mbit/s at 640 × 480 and 15 fps, and about 370 Mbit/s at 640 × 480 and 30 fps. IMU samples and wheel messages add only a few Mbit/s. Use a wired link, ideally Gigabit Ethernet, for the higher settings.

**Clock synchronization.** With `send_capture_time: true` (the default), every frame carries its capture time. The controller accepts a frame only when that time is at most 20 ms ahead of its own clock and at most 2 s old, so run NTP (for example chrony) to keep both computers on the same time. If you cannot synchronize the clocks, set `send_capture_time: false`: the controller then uses each frame's arrival time, as with the simulator. This needs no clock agreement and costs the network delay in accuracy.

**Tip:** On a sensor computer that runs ufw, open the ports for the controller with `sudo ufw allow from ROBOT_ADDRESS to any port 53333:53335 proto tcp`.

______________________________________________________________________

## 3. Install and Run

1. **Get the source** on the sensor computer:

   ```
   git clone https://github.com/Sodero-labs/device_bridge.git
   cd device_bridge
   ```

   You can also copy the `device_bridge` folder to the sensor computer by other means, for example with `scp -r` from your PC.

1. **Choose a configuration.** Copy the example closest to your hardware, for example `cp config/turtlebot3_d435.yaml config/my_robot.yaml`, and edit it as described in [Configuration File](#configuration-file). `config/turtlebot3_d435.yaml` serves a RealSense D435 and the IMU of a TurtleBot3 OpenCR board, with the wheel stream prepared but commented out; `config/simulated.yaml` needs no hardware.

1. **Install and start** the service:

   ```
   sudo deploy/install.sh config/my_robot.yaml
   ```

   The installer copies the program and your configuration to `/opt/sodero-device-bridge` (as `config.yaml`), creates a Python environment there and installs the `sodero-device-bridge` service. The service starts now and at every boot, and restarts 3 seconds after an error. It runs as the user who called `sudo`, with access to serial ports, USB devices and cameras.

1. **Follow the log** with `journalctl -u sodero-device-bridge -f` and look for the lines in [Log Lines](#log-lines).

1. **Check the streams** from another computer, as described in [Check from Another Computer](#check-from-another-computer).

To change a setting later, edit `/opt/sodero-device-bridge/config.yaml` and run `sudo systemctl restart sodero-device-bridge`.

Running `install.sh` again, for example after `git pull`, replaces `/opt/sodero-device-bridge/config.yaml` with the file you pass. Keep your configuration in your own file and pass it every time.

### Configuration File

The configuration names the robot, lists the devices on this computer and states which stream each device feeds. Every stream is optional; the bridge opens only the ports of the streams you configure.

```
robot_name: tb3              # the controller finds this robot's data under this name

network:                     # optional; these are the defaults
  bind: 0.0.0.0              # every interface, or this computer's LAN address
  command_port: 53333        # controller -> bridge: wheel commands
  state_port: 53334          # bridge -> controller: IMU samples and wheel states
  camera_port: 53335         # bridge -> controller: RGB-D frames and intrinsics

state_poll_hz: 200           # optional; how often the IMU and wheel devices are read

devices:                     # the hardware, each under a name you choose
  d435:
    driver: realsense        # a built-in driver
    serial: auto             # every other key is an option of the driver
    width: 424
    height: 240
    fps: 15
  opencr:
    driver: turtlebot3_opencr
    port: /dev/turtlebot3_opencr
    max_linear_speed: 0.15   # m/s
    max_angular_speed: 1.0   # rad/s

streams:                     # what the controller receives
  camera:
    device: d435
    frame_id: cam0_optical   # the camera frame named in the map bundle
    send_capture_time: true  # needs synchronized clocks; false = arrival time
  imu:
    device: opencr           # one device can feed several streams
  wheels:                    # only when the controller drives these wheels
    device: opencr
    command_timeout_s: 0.5   # stop the wheels when commands pause this long
```

| Key                                | Default        | Description                                                                                                                                            |
| ---------------------------------- | -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `robot_name`                       | required       | Name under which the bridge publishes. The Station's gateways use the same name.                                                                       |
| `network.bind`                     | `0.0.0.0`      | Address the bridge listens on. Enter the sensor computer's LAN address to restrict it to one interface.                                                |
| `network.camera_port`              | `53335`        | RGB-D frames. Must match the Camera gateway's **Port**.                                                                                                |
| `network.state_port`               | `53334`        | IMU samples and wheel states. Keep the default: the IMU and Actuator gateways expect it.                                                               |
| `network.command_port`             | `53333`        | Wheel commands. Keep the default.                                                                                                                      |
| `state_poll_hz`                    | `200`          | How often the IMU and wheel drivers are polled, per second                                                                                             |
| `devices.<name>.driver`            | required       | A [built-in driver](#4-built-in-drivers) or your own class as `package.module:Class`. All other keys of the block are passed to the driver as options. |
| `streams.camera.device`            | —              | The device that provides the camera                                                                                                                    |
| `streams.camera.frame_id`          | `cam0_optical` | Optical frame name sent with each frame, 1 to 15 bytes                                                                                                 |
| `streams.camera.send_capture_time` | `true`         | Send each frame's capture time. `false`: the controller uses the arrival time.                                                                         |
| `streams.imu.device`               | —              | The device that provides the IMU                                                                                                                       |
| `streams.wheels.device`            | —              | The device that drives the wheels. Leave the stream out when the controller drives its own base.                                                       |
| `streams.wheels.command_timeout_s` | `0.5`          | Stop the wheels when commands pause this long, in seconds                                                                                              |

Unknown keys are refused, so a typo stops the bridge with a clear message instead of being ignored. The configuration needs at least one device and one stream, and each stream must name a listed device that provides it.

**Tip:** Choose a `robot_name` of lowercase letters, digits and underscores that starts with a letter, such as `tb3`. Every Station node accepts such a name, so the gateway nodes can carry the same name.

### Log Lines

After a start with `config/turtlebot3_d435.yaml` (camera and IMU, no wheel stream), the log shows these lines (time stamps left out):

```
INFO device_bridge: device 'd435' (realsense) is open
INFO device_bridge: device 'opencr' (turtlebot3_opencr) is open
INFO device_bridge.bridge: camera 424x240 fx=303.22 fy=303.26 cx=216.20 cy=123.18 frame_id=cam0_optical (use these intrinsics in the controller's camera settings)
INFO device_bridge.bridge: serving robot 'tb3' on 0.0.0.0 (camera 53335, state 53334, command -)
INFO device_bridge: camera_pair 15.0/s, imu_state 50.0/s, sim_state 0.0/s, sim_command 0.0/s
```

| Line                                                              | Meaning                                                                                           |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `device '…' (…) is open`                                          | The driver has connected to its hardware.                                                         |
| `camera 424x240 fx=… fy=… cx=… cy=…`                              | The camera's resolution and intrinsics. Enter them in the Camera gateway (see [Camera](#camera)). |
| `serving robot 'tb3' on … (camera 53335, state 53334, command -)` | The robot name and the ports served. `-` marks a stream that is not configured.                   |
| `camera_pair 15.0/s, imu_state 50.0/s, …`                         | Message rates, every 10 seconds. `sim_command` counts the commands received from the controller.  |

If the configuration or a device fails, the log shows one `ERROR` line that names the problem, and the service tries again 3 seconds later.

### Check from Another Computer

`listen` receives the streams the way the controller does. Run it from a copy of the source on any computer on the same network, for example your PC:

```
cd device_bridge
python3 -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate
pip install numpy pyzmq PyYAML
python -m device_bridge.listen SENSOR_COMPUTER_ADDRESS --robot tb3
```

It prints one line per message kind with its rate and latest values, for example:

```
camera_info     1.0/s  width=424 height=240 fx=303.217 fy=303.257 cx=216.198 cy=123.175
camera_pair    15.0/s  424x240, depth valid 91%, median 1480 mm, capture age 9 ms (meaningful with synchronized clocks)
imu_state      50.0/s  gyro [+0.002, -0.001, +0.000] rad/s, |accel| 9.80 m/s^2
```

To test the wheels, add `--wheels` with one speed per wheel in rad/s, for example `--wheels 1.0 1.0 --seconds 2`. `listen` drives them for `--seconds` and then releases them the way the controller does.

`--wheels` moves the robot. Lift the wheels off the ground or give the robot room, and stop the Station's Actuator gateway for this robot first.

### Try Without Hardware

`config/simulated.yaml` serves a test-pattern camera, a slowly turning IMU and two ideal wheels under the robot name `tb3`. Use it to try the network, the Station's gateway settings and `listen` before the hardware is ready. Install it as a service, or run it in the foreground in the environment from the previous section:

```
sudo deploy/install.sh config/simulated.yaml     # as a service
python -m device_bridge config/simulated.yaml    # or in the foreground; stop with Ctrl+C
```

______________________________________________________________________

## 4. Built-in Drivers

The bridge comes with these drivers. They are ready to use and serve as examples: other cameras, IMUs and wheel boards connect through a driver that you add ([Write Device Bridge Drivers](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/extend/device_bridge_drivers/index.md)).

| Driver                 | Provides                     | Options (default)                                                                                                                                               |
| ---------------------- | ---------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `realsense`            | Camera                       | `serial` (`auto`), `width` (`424`), `height` (`240`), `fps` (`15`)                                                                                              |
| `turtlebot3_opencr`    | IMU and wheels (left, right) | `port` (`/dev/turtlebot3_opencr`), `poll_hz` (`100`, 20 to 100), `max_linear_speed` (`0.15` m/s, at most 0.22), `max_angular_speed` (`1.0` rad/s, at most 2.84) |
| `simulated_camera`     | Camera                       | `width` (`424`), `height` (`240`), `fps` (`15`)                                                                                                                 |
| `simulated_imu`        | IMU                          | `rate_hz` (`100`), `yaw_rate` (`0.1` rad/s)                                                                                                                     |
| `simulated_wheels`     | Wheels                       | `joints` (`2`), `rate_hz` (`100`)                                                                                                                               |
| `package.module:Class` | What the class provides      | Your own driver ([Write Device Bridge Drivers](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/extend/device_bridge_drivers/index.md))                                  |

- **`realsense`** reads Intel RealSense D400 cameras through the RealSense SDK and is tested with the D435. Depth is aligned to the color image, so both share the color camera's intrinsics. With `serial: auto`, exactly one camera must be connected; with several cameras, enter the serial number.
- **`turtlebot3_opencr`** drives the OpenCR board of a TurtleBot3 Burger running the ROBOTIS TurtleBot3 ROS 2 firmware. The board is both the wheel controller and the IMU, and its serial port can have only one owner, so one device feeds both the `imu` and the `wheels` stream. Wheel speeds are scaled down together to the configured limits, which keeps the path's curvature. If the bridge stops talking to the board, the firmware stops the wheels by itself within 0.5 s. Set `port` to the board's serial device (for example `/dev/ttyACM0`) when the default device name does not exist on your system.
- **`simulated_camera`**, **`simulated_imu`** and **`simulated_wheels`** stand in for hardware: a moving color pattern in front of a flat wall 2 m away, a level sensor turning slowly about its z axis, and joints that follow their velocity commands exactly.

______________________________________________________________________

## 5. Connect It on the Station Page

Start with the bridge running and `listen` showing its streams, then open the Station page (`http://ROBOT_ADDRESS`). The steps use the robot name `tb3`; use your bridge's `robot_name` instead.

**Names must match.** The Camera gateway's **Camera name**, the IMU gateway's **Robot in World** and the Actuator gateway's **Robot name** must all be exactly the bridge's `robot_name`. Each gateway takes only the data published under its name.

### Camera

1. Click **Add node**, choose **Gateway** › **Camera gateway** and name it after the robot, for example `tb3` (node `sodero.camera_gateway.tb3`).

1. In the **CAMERA GATEWAY** section of the inspector, enter:

   - **Camera name**: the bridge's `robot_name` (`tb3`). The bridge publishes its camera under the robot name; it has no separate camera name.
   - **Camera host**: `SENSOR_COMPUTER_ADDRESS`.
   - **Port**: `53335`, or the bridge's `network.camera_port`.

1. Enter the resolution and intrinsics from the bridge's `camera …` log line. A new Camera gateway computes its intrinsics from a field of view, as for a simulated camera, so for intrinsics its **CAMERA SETTINGS** show *horizontal fov deg* but not fx, fy, cx and cy. Load the calibrated values once with **Upload yaml** while the node is stopped:

   ```
   camera_gateway:
     camera:
       type: isaac_zmq              # the simulator's stream format, which the bridge speaks
       frame_id: cam0_optical       # the bridge's streams.camera.frame_id
       width: 424                   # resolution from the log line
       height: 240
       fps: 15
       isaac:
         robot_name: tb3            # Camera name: the bridge's robot_name
         host: SENSOR_COMPUTER_ADDRESS
         port: 53335
       intrinsics:
         mode: manual               # use fx, fy, cx, cy instead of a field of view
         fx: 303.22
         fy: 303.26
         cx: 216.20
         cy: 123.18
   ```

   After the upload, **CAMERA SETTINGS** shows these values and you can change them there later. Check that **Camera name**, **Camera host** and **Port** show your values.

1. Click **Start**.

Intrinsics belong to one resolution. After you change the bridge's `width`, `height` or camera, enter the new values from its log line.

**Tip:** In the [SSH workspace](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/ssh_workspace/overview/index.md), `sodero camera snapshot sodero.camera_gateway.tb3 --output frame.png` saves a picture from the gateway.

### IMU

1. Click **Add node**, choose **Gateway** › **IMU gateway** and name it after the robot (`tb3`).
1. In **IMU SETTINGS**, check that **Robot in World** is the bridge's `robot_name` (a new IMU gateway starts with its node name) and click **Save settings**.
1. Start the gateway.

The IMU gateway has no address field: it connects to the simulator address set for the controller, which must be the sensor computer ([Requirements](#2-requirements)).

### Wheels (Optional)

Only when the bridge serves a `wheels` stream:

1. Add an **Actuator gateway** and load a simulation `.gw` (`hardware.type: simulation`) whose joints are the bridge's wheels, in the same order (`turtlebot3_opencr`: left, then right).
1. In its **TARGET** section, click **Change**, enter **Robot name** `tb3` and **Sim host** `SENSOR_COMPUTER_ADDRESS`, and click **Done**.
1. Add **Strider** with your base's `.sddm` and connect its `servo_link` to the Actuator gateway's `servo_link`.
1. Drive slowly at first, with the wheels off the ground.

The bridge stops and releases the wheels when the controller switches its drive off and when commands pause for longer than `command_timeout_s`. Keep someone ready to stop the robot during the first runs.

### Navigation and Mounting

1. Add **Visual odometry**, **Localizer** and **Navigator** and connect them as for any robot: the Camera gateway's `camera` to Visual odometry and the Localizer, the IMU gateway's `imu` to Visual odometry, Visual odometry's (or Strider's) `odometry` to the Localizer, the Localizer's `localization` and `map` to the Navigator, and Strider's `mobile_base` to the Navigator.
1. Upload the map bundle (`.nav`) once to the Localizer. The Navigator uses the same shared bundle ([Load and Configure a Map](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/navigation/map_bundle/index.md)).

The bridge sends camera and IMU data in the sensors' own frames. Where the sensors sit on the robot, their mounting extrinsics, belongs in the map bundle ([Load and Configure a Map](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/navigation/map_bundle/#3-check-the-values-for-the-first-run)): measure the mounting and enter it there, and do not rotate data inside a driver. Keep the bridge's `frame_id`, the Camera gateway's *frame id* and the camera frame of the map bundle the same (default `cam0_optical`).

______________________________________________________________________

## 6. Troubleshooting

| Symptom                                                                                                          | Cause                                                                                                                                                                                                         | Fix                                                                                                                                                                    |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The service restarts every few seconds and the log shows one `ERROR` line                                        | A configuration or device problem named in that line, such as an unknown key, a stream without its device, `RealSense … is not connected` or `no reply from the board`                                        | Fix the configuration or the connection, then restart the service                                                                                                      |
| `listen` prints `no messages from … for robot '…'`                                                               | The bridge is not running, `--robot` differs from `robot_name`, or a firewall blocks the ports                                                                                                                | Check `systemctl status sodero-device-bridge`, use the name from the `serving robot` line, open TCP 53333–53335                                                        |
| Camera gateway: `Waiting for simulator at …:53335`                                                               | Wrong **Camera host** or **Port**, no camera stream, or a firewall                                                                                                                                            | Compare with the `serving robot` line and run `listen` from another computer                                                                                           |
| Camera gateway: `… publishes frames of camera(s) 'tb3' but none of camera '…'`                                   | **Camera name** differs from `robot_name`                                                                                                                                                                     | Set **Camera name** to `robot_name`, then Stop and Start                                                                                                               |
| Camera gateway: `Frames … are stale or carry capture times that do not match this Station's clock (clock skew?)` | The clocks differ: frames look more than 20 ms in the future or more than 2 s old                                                                                                                             | Synchronize the clocks with NTP, or set `send_capture_time: false` and restart the bridge                                                                              |
| Visual odometry drifts or the Localizer does not fit the map                                                     | Field-of-view intrinsics instead of the calibrated ones, or values for another resolution                                                                                                                     | Upload the intrinsics from the bridge's log line for the current resolution                                                                                            |
| The IMU gateway does not start: `Start the project World to provide the simulation IMU endpoint.`                | No simulator address is set for the controller                                                                                                                                                                | Have it set to the sensor computer ([Addresses Set for the Controller](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/gateways/simulation/#addresses-set-for-the-controller)) |
| The IMU gateway runs, but no IMU data arrives                                                                    | **Robot in World** differs from `robot_name`, the bridge has no `imu` stream (`state -`), or the controller's simulator address is another computer                                                           | Fix the name or the stream. The IMU gateway's log shows the address it connects to.                                                                                    |
| The wheels do not move                                                                                           | No `wheels` stream (`command -`), a different **Robot name**, commands that are not velocity commands (`modes … are not velocity control`), or the OpenCR motor power is off (`wheel motors are not powered`) | Add the stream, fix the name, drive Strider in **Twist** mode, switch on the motor power                                                                               |
| The wheels stop while driving; log: `no wheel command for 0.50 s: wheels stopped`                                | The safety watchdog: commands paused longer than `command_timeout_s`                                                                                                                                          | Use a wired link; raise `command_timeout_s` only with care                                                                                                             |
| The `camera_pair` rate stays below `fps`                                                                         | Not enough bandwidth (Wi-Fi), a USB 2 port or a busy sensor computer                                                                                                                                          | Use a wired link and a USB 3 port, or lower `width`, `height` or `fps`                                                                                                 |
| **Camera host** cannot be edited                                                                                 | A camera address is set for the controller; the gateway uses it in place of **Camera host**                                                                                                                   | Have it set to the sensor computer ([Addresses Set for the Controller](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/gateways/simulation/#addresses-set-for-the-controller)) |
# Stellar Designer

# Stellar Designer

**Stellar Designer** creates and edits the design documents of gateways and controllers: the robot's structure, its limits and safety settings, and how the gateway's actuators drive its joints or wheels. Each actuator gateway and controller node on the Station holds one document:

| Document | Describes                                                                      | Node             | Page                                                                                                                  |
| -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `.gw`    | The actuators and the hardware that drives them (EtherCAT drives or Isaac Sim) | Actuator gateway | [Gateway Designer (.gw)](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/gateways/gateway_designer/index.md)                  |
| `.sdd`   | Manipulator (serial arm)                                                       | Motion Studio    | [Manipulator (.sdd)](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/tutorials/stellar_designer/manipulator/index.md)         |
| `.sddm`  | Wheeled mobile base                                                            | Strider          | [Mobile Robot (.sddm)](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/tutorials/stellar_designer/mobile_robot/index.md)      |
| `.sdda`  | Articulated robot driven joint by joint (legged robots, humanoids)             | Articulation     | [Articulated Robot (.sdda)](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/tutorials/stellar_designer/articulation/index.md) |

A 3D model (`.glb`) for display is optional ([3D Model Creation](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/tutorials/stellar_designer/3dmodel_creation/index.md)). This page covers the controller documents. Gateway documents (`.gw`) are edited in the [Gateway Designer](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/gateways/gateway_designer/index.md), the part of Stellar Designer for `.gw` files, described with the gateways.

______________________________________________________________________

## 1. Open Stellar Designer

1. On the Station, select a controller node (Motion Studio, Strider or Articulation).
1. Click **Edit Stellar Designer** in the node's **DEFINITION** section.

Stellar Designer opens in a new tab with the node's document. Changes are saved back to the node automatically; in an Articulation document, click **Save configuration**. **Stop the node before you edit its document**; the new document takes effect the next time the node starts.

If a Motion Studio or Strider node has no document yet, Stellar Designer opens **Create robot definition**: choose a template of the robot type, or **Blank robot** for a manipulator, click **Next**, then **Create**. An Articulation node starts with a document of one joint.

| Robot type  | Templates                                                                                       |
| ----------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Manipulator | 2-axis two-bar arm, 4-axis SCARA, 4-axis cylindrical SCARA, 7-axis humanoid arm, Blank robot    |
| Mobile      | Differential drive 2WD, MiR250 differential, Skid steer 4WD, Mecanum 4WD, Swerve 4WD, Ackermann |

You can also import a document you already have with **Import** in the node's **DEFINITION** section ([Design Documents](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/station/design_documents/index.md)).

______________________________________________________________________

## 2. Screen Layout

Stellar Designer with a 6-axis arm

| Area        | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| ----------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Breadcrumb  | Where the document belongs: device / Station / node / file. The arrow returns to the Station.                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| Steps       | **01 Robot Structure** (or **Chassis Structure** for mobile robots), **02 Robot System Parameters**, **03 Actuator Mapping**, **04 Verification**. An Articulation document has two steps: **01 Joint configuration** and **02 Actuator Mapping**. Click a step to open it; you can go back and forth. |
| Left panel  | The joints (or wheels) of the robot, with their parameters                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| 3D view     | The robot as you define it. Drag to rotate, right-drag to pan, scroll to zoom. **Fit view** frames the robot; **Focus selection** frames the selected part.                                                                                                                                            |
| Right panel | Details of the selection, such as constraints, or the parameters of the current step                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| Units       | `mm / g / deg` or `m / kg / radian`. Display only; documents store SI units.                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |

### Display Menu

The Display menu

**Display** in the 3D view switches between **Skeleton** (joint frames and links as lines) and **3D Model**, and shows or hides **Joint frames**, **Grid** and **Axis gizmo**. **Load.glb** attaches the robot's 3D model, a GLB file, to the document; Motion Studio then shows the robot with it ([3D Model Creation](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/tutorials/stellar_designer/3dmodel_creation/index.md)).

______________________________________________________________________

## 3. Workflow

1. **Structure.** Define the joints (manipulator) or the chassis and wheels (mobile robot).
1. **System parameters.** Enter the robot-wide values: payload, gravity, speed limits, goal tolerances, safety margins.
1. **Actuator mapping.** Connect the gateway's actuators to the joints or wheels, with their transmission factors.
1. **Verification.** Click **Verify**. When all checks pass, the document is ready; **Export** saves a copy to your computer.

An Articulation document has only the joints with their limits and the actuator mapping ([Articulated Robot](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/tutorials/stellar_designer/articulation/index.md)).

Then start the node on the Station and try the robot, in simulation first.

# Manipulator (.sdd)

This guide walks through the four steps of a manipulator document. The document belongs to a Motion Studio node (`sodero.mmc.NAME`), which drives the arm through an actuator gateway. The pictures show a 6-axis arm, the same arm whose 3D model is assembled in [3D Model Creation](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/tutorials/stellar_designer/3dmodel_creation/index.md). No `.sdd` document of this arm is provided: enter the data of your own arm.

______________________________________________________________________

## Before You Start

1. On the Station, add a **Controller › Motion Studio** node, for example `arm`, and an **Actuator gateway** for its motors ([Nodes and Connections](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/station/nodes_and_connections/index.md)).
1. Select the Motion Studio node and click **Edit Stellar Designer**. For a new node, choose a template or **Blank robot** in **Create robot definition**.

You need the arm's kinematics as **DH parameters** (from its datasheet or CAD), its joint limits, and, for accurate gravity compensation and collision detection, the mass properties of its links.

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 1: Robot Structure

Robot Structure: joints, DH parameters and constraints

Step **01 Robot Structure** ① shows the **Joint Section**: the joints from the base to the tool flange.

1. Click **Add joint** ⑥ to add a joint at the end of the chain. The trash icon removes a joint.
1. Open a joint ② and choose its **Joint Type** ③: rotation or translation about the joint's X, Y or Z axis.
1. Enter its **DH PARAMETERS** ④: **DH (Theta)**, **DH (D)**, **DH (A)** and **DH (Alpha)**. The 3D view updates as you type.
1. Under **ADVANCED SETTINGS**:
   - **Dynamics**: the mass, center of mass and inertia of the link that moves with this joint.
   - **Constraints** ⑤: opens the joint's constraints in the right panel ⑧.
1. Use **JOG** **+** / **−** to move the joint in the 3D view and check its direction. **Jog Reset** returns all joints to zero.

**Joint constraints** ⑧:

| Group                   | Fields                         | Meaning                                                                  |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **JOINT LIMITS**        | Lower Limit, Upper Limit       | Range of motion of the joint                                             |
| **KINEMATIC LIMITS**    | Max Speed, Max Accel, Max Jerk | Limits of trajectories in joint space                                    |
| **FRICTION PARAMETERS** | w1, f1, w2, f2, Max Friction   | Friction model used by the dynamics (velocity and torque breakpoints)    |
| **COLLISION THRESHOLD** | Collision Threshold            | Residual torque above which the controller detects a collision and stops |
| **GOAL TOLERANCE**      | Joint Goal                     | How close a joint must be for a motion to count as finished              |

**Display** ⑦ switches the 3D view between the skeleton and the robot's 3D model ([Stellar Designer](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/tutorials/stellar_designer/introduction/#display-menu)).

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 2: Robot System Parameters

General

Safety (Advanced)

**General**:

| Group              | Fields                                           | Meaning                                                                                                                                |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **ROBOT**          | Arm reach, Max payload, Max allowable inertia    | Size and payload rating of the arm                                                                                                     |
| **ENVIRONMENT**    | Gravity vector                                   | Direction and size of gravity in the base frame; `(0, 0, -9.81) m/s²` for a floor-mounted arm. Change it for wall or ceiling mounting. |
| **MOTION**         | Task space limit: Max speed, Max accel, Max jerk | Limits of the tool in Cartesian motions                                                                                                |
| **GOAL TOLERANCE** | Position, Orientation                            | How close the tool must be for a Cartesian motion to count as finished                                                                 |

**Safety (Advanced)**:

| Group               | Fields                                                          | Meaning                                                                                                                                              |
| ------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **WARNING**         | Revolute margin, Prismatic margin, Velocity ratio, Torque ratio | Distance to a joint limit, or fraction of a speed or torque limit, at which the controller warns                                                     |
| **PROTECTIVE STOP** | the same fields                                                 | Thresholds at which the controller stops the robot                                                                                                   |
| **EMERGENCY STOP**  | Comm timeout, Max overrun                                       | Emergency stop when the gateway's feedback is missing for longer than **Comm timeout**, or the control loop overruns for longer than **Max overrun** |
|                     | Clear grace                                                     | After a protective stop is cleared, joint position limits are not checked for this time, so the robot can move back from the limit                   |

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 3: Actuator Mapping

Six actuators, each driving one joint

The canvas shows the gateway's actuators (top) and the robot's joints (bottom).

1. Drag from an actuator's connector to a joint's connector to connect them. A new arm starts with Actuator *n* connected to Joint *n*.
1. In the right panel, set the **INFLUENCE FACTOR** of each connection: how many joint units one actuator unit moves, after the gear. Use `1` for a direct joint, a negative value to reverse the direction, and several connections for coupled joints (such as a differential wrist).
1. The trash icon removes a connection.

The gear ratio of each motor belongs to the gateway's document, not here ([Gateway Designer](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/gateways/gateway_designer/index.md)).

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 4: Verification

1. Click **Verify**. Stellar Designer checks the robot structure, the system parameters, the actuator mapping and the configuration files of the document.
1. Open a group to see each check. Fix any errors and click **Verify again**.

All checks passed

**Export .sdd** saves a copy of the document to your computer, for backup or for other Stations.

______________________________________________________________________

## Try the Arm

1. Return to the Station, connect the Motion Studio node's `servo_link` to the gateway, and start the gateway and the Motion Studio node.
1. Open **Stellar Motion Studio** from the node and jog each joint slowly. Check that every joint moves in the direction and by the angle you expect ([Motion Studio](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/controllers/motion_studio/index.md)).

**Tip:** Try a new document in Isaac Sim first ([Virtual Simulation](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/virtual_simulation/introduction/index.md)). Errors in DH parameters or joint directions are easy to see there and harmless.

# Mobile Robot (.sddm)

This tutorial builds the document of a wheeled mobile base, using the Clearpath Jackal (skid steer, four wheels) of the [Quick Start](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/get_started/quick_start/index.md). The document belongs to a Strider node (`sodero.mlc.NAME`).

______________________________________________________________________

## Before You Start

1. On the Station, add a **Controller › Strider** node, for example `jackal`, and an **Actuator gateway** for its wheel motors ([Nodes and Connections](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/station/nodes_and_connections/index.md)).
1. Select the Strider node and click **Edit Stellar Designer**.
1. In **Create robot definition**, choose the template that matches your drive:

| Template               | Drive                                            |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| Differential drive 2WD | Two driven wheels and casters                    |
| MiR250 differential    | Differential drive of a MiR250                   |
| Skid steer 4WD         | Four fixed driven wheels that slide when turning |
| Mecanum 4WD            | Four mecanum wheels, omnidirectional             |
| Swerve 4WD             | Four steered and driven wheels                   |
| Ackermann              | Car-like steering                                |

The template sets the drive type, which decides how body velocities become wheel commands. Then change its dimensions to those of your robot.

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 1: Chassis Structure

Chassis Structure of a skid-steer base

Step **01 Chassis Structure** ① shows the body and the wheels of the base.

**Body** ②:

| Field                             | Meaning                                                                      |
| --------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Template**                      | The drive type of the template, for example `skid_steer_4` (read-only)       |
| **Length**, **Width**, **Height** | Outer dimensions of the body                                                 |
| **Base Origin Z**                 | Height of the robot's base frame above the floor (normally the wheel radius) |
| **Track Width**                   | Distance between the left and right wheels of a differential drive           |

**Wheels** ③: one card per wheel, for example **Wheel-fl**. The template sets the wheel names and their roles:

| Template                                    | Wheels                                                 | Role                                      |
| ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------- |
| Differential drive 2WD, MiR250 differential | `left`, `right`                                        | `drive`                                   |
| Skid steer 4WD, Mecanum 4WD                 | `fl`, `fr`, `rl`, `rr`                                 | `drive`                                   |
| Swerve 4WD                                  | `fl`, `fr`, `rl`, `rr`                                 | `drive_steer`                             |
| Ackermann                                   | `front_left`, `front_right`, `rear_left`, `rear_right` | `steer` at the front, `drive` at the rear |

| Field                                    | Meaning                                                                                                   |
| ---------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Role**                                 | Read-only, set by the template: `drive` (driven), `steer` (steered) or `drive_steer` (driven and steered) |
| **Radius**, **Width**                    | Wheel size                                                                                                |
| **Offset X**, **Offset Y**, **Offset Z** | Wheel position relative to the base frame (X forward, Y left)                                             |

**Constraints** ④ opens the wheel's drive limits in the right panel ⑥: **max_speed** and **max_accel** of the wheel.

The constraints of the front-left wheel, with its diameter and width in the 3D view

**Display** ⑤ changes the 3D view; the unit menu ⑦ changes the display units.

Skid-steer wheels slide sideways when the robot turns, so the robot turns less than the wheel speeds suggest. The skid-steer kinematics use the wheels' **Offset Y**: turn the robot in place by a known angle and increase the left and right **Offset Y** until the odometry matches the real turn. The simulated Jackal of the Quick Start, for example, uses an effective **Offset Y** of 0.441 m.

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 2: Robot System Parameters

Robot System Parameters of the Jackal

| Group           | Fields                                                                   | Meaning                                                                   |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **ROBOT**       | Total mass, Max payload, Center of mass, Body inertia                    | Mass properties of the robot                                              |
| **ENVIRONMENT** | Gravity vector                                                           | Normally `(0, 0, -9.81) m/s²`                                             |
| **MOTION**      | Max linear speed, Max angular speed, Max linear accel, Max angular accel | Limits of the body velocity. Strider and the Navigator never exceed them. |

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 3: Actuator Mapping

Four actuators driving the four wheels

Connect each actuator of the gateway to the wheel it drives (or steers), as for a manipulator ([Manipulator › Actuator Mapping](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/tutorials/stellar_designer/manipulator/#step-3-actuator-mapping)). The order must match the gateway: in the Jackal's gateway, actuator 1 is the front-left wheel, 2 front-right, 3 rear-left, 4 rear-right.

A mobile base uses the mapping only to know which actuator drives which wheel; leave the **INFLUENCE FACTOR** at `1`. The wheel kinematics already account for the left and right side. If a real wheel still turns the wrong way, invert the motor's direction in its drive, for example by writing the drive's polarity parameter as a start-up SDO ([EtherCAT Gateway](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/gateways/ethercat/#ethercat-tab)).

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 4: Verification

Click **Verify**. Stellar Designer checks the chassis structure, the system parameters, the actuator mapping and the configuration files.

All checks passed: skid steer, 4 wheels, 4 actuators

**Export .sddm** saves a copy of the document to your computer.

______________________________________________________________________

## Try the Robot

Start the gateway and the Strider node, open Strider, choose **Twist**, switch the servo on and drive slowly ([Strider](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/controllers/strider/index.md)). Check that:

- **Forward** drives forward and every wheel turns the right way,
- **Turn Left** turns counterclockwise (seen from above),
- the odometry on the **Status** page matches the distance and angle actually driven.

# Articulated Robot (.sdda)

This tutorial builds the document of a robot whose joints are driven one by one, using a four-legged robot with twelve joints as the example. The document belongs to an Articulation node (`sodero.amc.NAME`). Unlike a manipulator or mobile base document, it describes no kinematics: only the joints, their limits and how the gateway's actuators drive them. How the controller uses the document is described in [Articulation](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/controllers/articulation/index.md).

______________________________________________________________________

## Before You Start

1. On the Station, add a **Controller › Articulation** node, for example `quadruped`, and an **Actuator gateway** for its motors ([Nodes and Connections](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/station/nodes_and_connections/index.md)).
1. Connect the Articulation node's `servo_link` to the gateway.
1. Select the Articulation node and click **Edit Stellar Designer**.

A new Articulation node starts with one joint, `joint_1`. There are no templates; you add the joints of your robot one by one.

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 1: Joint Configuration

Joint configuration of a four-legged robot with twelve joints

Step **01 Joint configuration** ① shows the controller settings on the left and the joints on the right.

**Controller**:

| Field                    | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| ------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Controller subsystem** | The ID of the node. The Station fills it in.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| **Actuator gateway**     | The gateway connected to the node's `servo_link`. The Station fills it in.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **Drive mode** ②         | **Position targets**: the controller bounds the joint targets, and the drive (or the simulated joint) follows them with its own position control. Set a matching effort limit in the drive or the simulator. **Bounded PD torque**: the controller computes a torque from each joint's **Kp** and **Kd** and clamps it to the joint's torque limit. |

**Joints**: **Add joint** ③ adds a joint at the end of the list, up to 64 joints. Open a joint ④ to edit it:

| Field                  | Meaning                                                              |
| ---------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Name**               | A unique name of letters, digits and underscores                     |
| **Min**, **Max** (rad) | Range of motion. Targets outside it are refused.                     |
| **Speed** (rad/s)      | Velocity limit, also the reference for the jog speed in Articulation |
| **Torque** (N·m)       | Torque limit                                                         |
| **Offset** (rad)       | Joint position at actuator position zero                             |
| **Kp**, **Kd**         | Stiffness and damping, shown in **Bounded PD torque** mode           |

**Move up** moves a joint one place up and **Remove** deletes it.

Each leg of the example robot (`fl`, `fr`, `rl`, `rr`) has a hip, a thigh and a calf joint, named for example `fl_hip`. The list runs leg by leg: `fl_hip`, `fl_thigh`, `fl_calf`, then the joints of `fr`, `rl` and `rr`. The example uses these values; enter those of your own robot:

|                   | Hip  | Thigh | Calf |
| ----------------- | ---- | ----- | ---- |
| **Min** (rad)     | −0.8 | −1.0  | −2.7 |
| **Max** (rad)     | 0.8  | 3.0   | −0.9 |
| **Speed** (rad/s) | 20   | 20    | 20   |
| **Torque** (N·m)  | 25   | 25    | 35   |

**Joint order matters.** Commands and feedback follow the order of the list. A program that sends joint targets must use the same order: Legged locomotion, for example, compares the joint names and their order with its walking policy and does not start if they differ (*The controller joint order does not match the policy manifest.*).

**Save configuration** ⑤ saves the document to the node; the button shows **Saved** when there is nothing left to save. Stellar Designer also saves when you return to the Station.

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 2: Actuator Mapping

Twelve actuators, each driving one joint

The canvas ① shows the gateway's actuators (top) and the joints (bottom); the right panel ② lists the **INFLUENCE FACTOR** of each connection. Every joint you add starts connected to the actuator with the same number, with factor `1`.

Change the mapping as for a manipulator ([Manipulator › Actuator Mapping](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/tutorials/stellar_designer/manipulator/#step-3-actuator-mapping)): drag from an actuator's connector to a joint's connector, set the influence factor, and use a negative factor to reverse a direction. Several connections describe coupled joints. The mapping uses as many actuators as there are joints, and it must be invertible: every set of joint targets must correspond to exactly one set of actuator commands.

Actuator *n* here is actuator *n* of the gateway. The gateway must provide at least as many actuators as the document has joints.

______________________________________________________________________

## Save a Copy

To save the document to your computer, click the Stellar mark at the top left and choose **Definition › Download .sdda**. You can import the file into another Articulation node with **Import .sdda** ([Design Documents](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/station/design_documents/index.md)).

______________________________________________________________________

## Try the Robot

**Real hardware moves.** Support a legged robot so that its feet are off the ground, keep the area clear and keep the emergency stop within reach.

Start the gateway, then the Articulation node, and click **Articulation** in the node's **CONTROL** section ([Articulation](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/controllers/articulation/index.md)). Switch the servo on and jog each joint at a low speed. Check that:

- each joint moves in the expected direction,
- each joint stops at its limits,
- the joint monitor shows the expected angles in a known pose. Correct a joint's zero with **Offset**, or with **Set origin** in Articulation.

This guide ends with this manual joint test. A program that sends joint targets, such as Legged locomotion with a walking policy, needs its own preparation, which this documentation does not cover: its joint names and order must match the document ([Step 1](#step-1-joint-configuration)), and it must be tested with the robot supported off the ground.

# 3D Model Creation

This tutorial assembles the 3D model of a robot arm for display in Stellar Designer and Motion Studio. **It is optional.** The model is for visualization only: the kinematics come from the DH parameters of the `.sdd` document, not from the model, and every robot runs without one. You can skip this page and add a model later.

The example is a 6-axis manipulator. Download its parts and unzip them:

- **[example_manipulator_parts.zip](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/tutorials/stellar_designer/3dmodel_creation/models/example_manipulator_parts.zip)**

The example manipulator

For your own robot you need one 3D model file per link, exported from your CAD design, and the robot's DH parameters.

The steps use [Blender](https://www.blender.org/download/), which reads most common 3D formats. Any other 3D tool works as long as it produces the same object names, hierarchy and file format.

______________________________________________________________________

## 1. Prepare the Scene in Blender

### Clear the Scene

Open Blender and delete the default `Camera`, `Cube` and `Light`.

### Naming Conventions

| Part       | Name               |
| ---------- | ------------------ |
| Base joint | `J0`               |
| Base link  | `link0`            |
| Joints     | `J1` to `Jn`       |
| Links      | `link1` to `linkn` |

`n` is the number of joints, 6 in this example.

### Create the Joints

Click **Add › Empty › Plain Axes** to add an axis object. Add seven of them and rename them `J0` to `J6`. Stellar Designer finds the joints by these names, so each name must be `J` followed by its number.

### Import the Links

Click **File › Import › Wavefront (.obj)**, open the folder of the unzipped parts and import all seven parts with the import settings shown above. The scene then looks like the last picture.

Select `link0` and set **Rotation X** to `0`: the part stands upright. Repeat this for the other parts.

### Attach Each Link to Its Joint

Select `link0` and Shift-drag it onto `J0`, so that `link0` sits under `J0`. Repeat this for the other links.

______________________________________________________________________

## 2. Build the Hierarchy

The robot is a serial chain: each joint is a child of the previous joint, and each link is a child of its joint.

```
World
└── J0
    ├── link0
    └── J1
        ├── link1
        └── J2
            ├── link2
            └── J3
                ├── link3
                └── J4
                    ├── link4
                    └── J5
                        ├── link5
                        └── J6
                            └── link6
```

Select `J1` and Shift-drag it onto `J0`: `J1` and `link1` are now under `J0`. Repeat this for the other joints.

| Item               | Description              |
| ------------------ | ------------------------ |
| `World`            | The scene of the 3D tool |
| `J0` to `Jn`       | Joint nodes              |
| `link0` to `linkn` | Link models              |

Each joint `Jn` must be a child of the previous joint, and each link `linkn` a child of its joint `Jn`. With a different hierarchy the links do not move with their joints.

______________________________________________________________________

## 3. Match the DH Parameters

The joint frames in Blender must match the DH parameters of the robot in Stellar Designer.

### DH Convention

Stellar Designer applies the four DH parameters of a joint in this fixed order:

1. Rotation about Z by θ (theta)
1. Translation along Z by d
1. Translation along X by a
1. Rotation about X by α (alpha)

### Place the Joints

J2 placed 0.205 m above J1

Joint J1 of the example has θ = 0, d = 205 mm, a = 0 and α = 0 in Stellar Designer, so the frame of J2 sits 205 mm above J1 along Z.

1. Select `J2` and set **Location Z** to `0.205`. `link2` and everything under `J2` moves up.
1. Set **Location Z** of `J3` to `0.27` and of `J5` to `0.23`. The model then looks like the last picture below.

For your own robot, the parts may not line up with the joint axes of the DH parameters. In that case, move the mesh itself in your CAD program. In the assembled pose, the base is at (0, 0, 0) and every joint is at 0.

### Joint Axes

- Stellar Designer turns each `Jn` about one of its own local axes: the axis of the joint's **Joint Type** in Stellar Designer (**Rotation X**, **Rotation Y** or **Rotation Z**). Orient each `Jn` so that this axis is the joint's axis of rotation.
- Rotate in the joint's local axes, not in the world axes.

______________________________________________________________________

## 4. Export the Model

1. Choose **File › Export › glTF 2.0 (.glb/.gltf)**.
1. In the export window, set **Format** to **glTF Binary (.glb)** and, under **Transform**, clear **+Y Up**.

Clear **+Y Up**. Otherwise Blender converts the model to a Y-up coordinate system, and it appears rotated in Stellar Designer.

The finished files of this example: **[.blend](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/tutorials/stellar_designer/3dmodel_creation/models/example_manipulator_assembly_vis.blend)** and **[.glb](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/tutorials/stellar_designer/3dmodel_creation/models/example_manipulator_assembly_vis.glb)**.

______________________________________________________________________

## 5. Load the Model in Stellar Designer

Open the robot's document in Stellar Designer, click **Display** in the 3D view and choose **Load.glb** ([Stellar Designer](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/tutorials/stellar_designer/introduction/#display-menu)). Switch **Representation** to **3D Model**: each link moves with its joint when you jog the joints in **Robot Structure**. Motion Studio then shows the robot with this model.

Stellar Designer uses only the `.glb` file.
# Simulation

# Virtual Simulation with Isaac Sim

The example scene of the Quick Start: a Clearpath Jackal and a Clearpath Dingo in a warehouse

[NVIDIA Isaac Sim](https://developer.nvidia.com/isaac/sim) is a robotics simulator with physically based rendering and GPU physics. With the **Isaac Bridge** extension, Isaac Sim becomes the simulator of Stellar X: the controllers on the Station drive robots in Isaac Sim through simulation gateways, with the same commands they send to real motors.

______________________________________________________________________

## How It Works

```
flowchart TB
    subgraph SX ["Stellar X · Stellar Station"]
        CTRL["Controllers<br>Motion Studio · Strider · Articulation"] --> AG["Simulation gateways<br>(actuator)"]
        IG["IMU gateways"]
        CG["Camera gateways"]
    end
    subgraph PC ["Isaac Sim computer"]
        IB["Isaac Bridge extension"] --- ST["Scene<br>robots · cameras"]
    end
    AG -- "joint commands · 53333" --> IB
    IB -- "joint states · 53334" --> AG
    IB -- "IMU · 53334" --> IG
    IB -- "RGB-D frames · 53335" --> CG
```

- **Gateways connect the simulator.** A simulation gateway replaces the fieldbus with the network connection to Isaac Sim. The controllers, their documents and your applications are the same as for the real robot. On the real robot you also verify the actuator mapping, calibration, limits and sensor settings.
- **Simulated joints behave like servo drives.** Each joint receives position, velocity or torque commands and reports its position, velocity and torque, like a drive with its motor and encoder.
- **Cameras and IMUs** of the scene are served to the Station's camera and IMU gateways, so localization, navigation and walking controllers run on simulated sensors.
- **Several robots** can share one scene. Each robot has a unique name, and each gateway on the Station names the robot it drives.

What you can do in simulation:

- Check kinematics, joint directions and limits before the first power-on of a real robot.
- Develop and test applications, navigation and mission logic without hardware.
- Test multi-robot scenarios and sites that do not exist yet.

______________________________________________________________________

## Requirements

| Item              | Requirement                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Isaac Sim         | 6.0, on Linux or Windows ([Isaac Sim requirements and installation](https://docs.isaacsim.omniverse.nvidia.com/latest/installation/index.html)). Isaac Bridge 1.0.0 is verified with Isaac Sim 6.0 ([Compatibility](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/reference/compatibility/index.md)).                                                                   |
| Isaac Bridge      | The Sodero extension for Isaac Sim ([Install Isaac Bridge](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/virtual_simulation/extension_installation/index.md))                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| Network           | Stellar X and the Isaac Sim computer on the same network; Stellar X must reach the Isaac Sim computer on TCP ports 53333–53335                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| Simulator address | Only for simulated IMUs. The IMU gateway has no address field: it connects to the simulator address set for the controller, which must be the Isaac Sim computer ([Addresses Set for the Controller](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/gateways/simulation/#addresses-set-for-the-controller)). Actuator and camera gateways have their own address fields. |
| Clock             | Both computers synchronized with a time server (NTP), when you use cameras                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |

______________________________________________________________________

## Steps

| Step                                                                        | Page                                                                                                               |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| 1. Install Isaac Sim and the Isaac Bridge extension                         | [Install Isaac Bridge](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/virtual_simulation/extension_installation/index.md) |
| 2. Prepare the robot in the scene: articulation, name, joint order, cameras | [Prepare the Robot](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/virtual_simulation/robot_setup/index.md)               |
| 3. Point the Station's gateways at Isaac Sim and run                        | [Connect to Stellar Station](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/virtual_simulation/connect_station/index.md)  |
