Any point-cloud tool, such as CloudCompare or Open3D, can do the steps below.

______________________________________________________________________

## 1. Choose the Coordinate Frames

Choose the `map` frame of your site: x and y horizontal, z up, the floor at z = 0, in meters. All frames, and why the camera height is measured from the floor, are explained in [Localization and Navigation › Coordinate Frames](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/navigation/overview/#2-coordinate-frames).

______________________________________________________________________

## 2. Get a Point Cloud

Collect points on every surface the camera will see, in the `map` frame of [step 1](#1-choose-the-coordinate-frames):

- **3D model:** sample points on the surfaces of the site's model, for example the USD world of your Isaac Sim scene, with normals and colors where available. When the map frame is the world frame, poses in the simulator and on the map are the same.
- **3D scan:** scan the real site with a laser scanner or by photogrammetry, and level the scan so that the floor lies at z = 0.

______________________________________________________________________

## 3. Clean and Export the PLY

1. Remove people, vehicles and other objects that move, stray points and everything outside the site.
1. Downsample to a point spacing of 2 to 5 cm, at most 2 million points; the Localizer reduces the map to `map.voxel_size` (5 cm by default) anyway.
1. Export a binary little-endian PLY with `float` x, y, z, optional normals and `uchar` colors: points only, no faces and no extra fields ([Point Cloud](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/navigation/map_bundle_format/#point-cloud-mapmap_idply)).

______________________________________________________________________

## 4. Make the Occupancy Grid

1. Pick the resolution (typically 0.05 m) and a rectangle that covers the cloud with a margin. Its lower-left corner is the `origin`; width and height are its size divided by the resolution, rounded up.
1. Mark a cell **occupied** (0) when it holds points in the height band the robot can hit, from just above the floor to just above the robot, for example 0.05 to 0.65 m.
1. Mark a cell **free** (254) when it holds floor points and no obstacle, and every other cell **unknown** (205).
1. Write the PGM with its top row at the largest y, then the grid YAML ([Occupancy Grid](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/navigation/map_bundle_format/#occupancy-grid-mapmap_idyaml-and-mapmap_idpgm)). Record the height band in `meta.yaml` as `z_slice`.

**Tip:** Compare the PGM with a top view of the point cloud. The walls must line up; a grid mirrored top to bottom was written bottom row first.

______________________________________________________________________

## 5. Write the YAML Files

Choose a map ID, name the three map files after it, and write the five YAML files: `meta.yaml`, `localizer.yaml`, `navigator.yaml`, `extrinsics.yaml` and `initial_pose.yaml` ([Files](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/navigation/map_bundle_format/#files)). Copy the width, height, resolution and origin of the grid into `meta.yaml` without rounding.

Start `navigator.yaml` from the file of a working bundle, such as the warehouse example of [Navigate in Simulation](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/navigation/simulation_tutorial/index.md), and change values only.

______________________________________________________________________

## 6. Measure the Camera Mounting

Measure the camera's optical center from `base_link`: x forward and y left from the base origin, z up from the floor. Measure its downward tilt and take the quaternion from [extrinsics.yaml](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/navigation/map_bundle_format/#extrinsicsyaml). Set `camera_frame_id` and the edge's `child` to the camera node's `frame_id`.

______________________________________________________________________

## 7. Pack the Bundle

```
# build/site.nav/ holds the five YAML files and map/
tar -czf site.nav.tgz -C build site.nav   # file for the Station page
cp site.nav.tgz site.nav                  # the same file, named for sodero maps upload
tar -tzf site.nav                         # every entry starts with site.nav/
```

Do not pack with `tar -czf site.nav.tgz -C build/site.nav .`: the `./` entry it adds is refused. Archive entries with hidden names, such as files some archivers add on macOS, are refused too.

______________________________________________________________________

## 8. Check the Bundle

The Station page checks the archive's layout when you upload it. The CLI preview checks every rule of the format without changing anything, so preview a new bundle from the [SSH workspace](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/ssh_workspace/overview/index.md) first:

```
sodero navigation get --node sodero.localizer                           # note "sha256"
sodero maps upload site.nav --node sodero.localizer --if-sha256 SHA256  # preview only, without --execute
```

The preview reports the first problem it finds ([Validation Errors](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/navigation/map_bundle_format/#validation-errors)).

### Checklist

- The `map` frame has the floor at z = 0, and the point cloud and the grid use the same coordinates.
- The grid files are `map/MAP_ID.pgm` and `map/MAP_ID.yaml`, and `meta.yaml` repeats their width, height, resolution and origin exactly.
- The PLY holds only x, y, z with optional normals and colors, and at most 2 million points.
- The grid YAML has exactly six keys, `negate` is 0 or 1, and `free_thresh` is below `occupied_thresh`.
- `camera_frame_id` matches the camera node's `frame_id`, the edges use `quat [x, y, z, w]`, and the camera height is measured from the floor.
- `initial_pose.yaml` gives the pose of `base_link`, with yaw in radians.
- `navigator.yaml` is complete, with your robot's `robot_radius` and speed limits.
- The archive is a gzip tar with one top folder, at most 64 MiB, and the CLI preview reports no problem.
- In simulation, the localization status reaches **Healthy** and the robot reaches a nearby goal before you drive the real robot.

Then upload the bundle: [Load and Configure a Map](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/navigation/map_bundle/index.md).

# Load and Configure a Map

A **map bundle** (`.nav`) is one file that carries the map of one site together with the settings to localize and navigate in it. You upload it once to the **Localizer**; the **Navigator** uses the same bundle, and **Visual odometry** uses its camera calibration. This page loads a finished bundle, checks the values for the first run and starts the nodes.

| You want to                                                             | Page                                                                                                  |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Load a finished bundle, such as the warehouse example                   | This page                                                                                             |
| Make a bundle for your own site                                         | [Create a Map from Your Site](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/navigation/create_map/index.md) |
| Look up every file and key of the format, and the messages of its check | [Map Bundle Format](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/navigation/map_bundle_format/index.md)    |

Stellar Station does not build maps on the robot; there is no SLAM. A bundle is made beforehand from a 3D model or a 3D scan of the site.

______________________________________________________________________

## 1. What You Need

- **The bundle file**, for example [warehouse.nav.tgz](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/navigation/simulation_tutorial/files/warehouse.nav.tgz) of [Navigate in Simulation](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/navigation/simulation_tutorial/index.md). The Station page accepts an archive of the bundle folder with a name ending in `.tar.gz`, `.tgz`, `.tar` or `.zip`. The CLI needs a gzip-compressed tar with a name ending in `.nav`: a `.tgz` bundle is such a file, so you can copy `site.nav.tgz` to `site.nav`.
- **A Localizer node** (`sodero.localizer`) and, to drive to goals, a **Navigator node** (`sodero.navigator`), connected as in [Localization and Navigation › Set Up Navigation](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/navigation/overview/#3-set-up-navigation).

The bundle contains five settings files and three map files:

| File                              | Contents                                                 | Read by                                |
| --------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| `meta.yaml`                       | The map ID and a description of the grid                 | Localizer and Navigator                |
| `localizer.yaml`                  | Localizer settings, including the point-cloud file       | Localizer                              |
| `navigator.yaml`                  | Navigator settings: robot size, speeds, tolerances       | Navigator                              |
| `extrinsics.yaml`                 | Where the camera is mounted on the robot                 | Localizer and Visual odometry          |
| `initial_pose.yaml`               | The starting pose of the robot on the map                | Localizer                              |
| `map/MAP_ID.ply`, `.pgm`, `.yaml` | The 3D point cloud and the 2D occupancy grid of the site | Localizer; Navigator and the map views |

______________________________________________________________________

## 2. Upload the Bundle

The Localizer and the Navigator share one bundle, so one upload to the Localizer serves both.

### Station Page

1. Stop the Localizer and the nodes that use its bundle (Navigator, Visual odometry).
1. Select the Localizer node. In the inspector's **LOCALIZER** section, click **Upload .nav** and choose `site.nav.tgz`.
1. The section shows the file name, and **NAVIGATION SETTINGS** lists the settings of the bundle.

The page checks the archive's layout. The CLI preview below checks every rule of the format, so preview a bundle you built yourself with the CLI before you upload it on the page.

### sodero CLI

```
sodero runtime node stop sodero.navigator --execute
sodero runtime node stop sodero.localizer --execute
sodero navigation get --node sodero.localizer                                     # note "sha256"
sodero maps upload site.nav --node sodero.localizer --if-sha256 SHA256            # preview: checks the bundle
sodero maps upload site.nav --node sodero.localizer --if-sha256 SHA256 --execute  # attach it
sodero runtime node start sodero.localizer --execute
sodero runtime node start sodero.navigator --execute
```

- With Visual odometry, also stop `sodero.visual_odometry` before the upload, and start it again before the Localizer.
- The file name must end in `.nav`, and the file may be at most 64 MiB.
- The preview reports the first problem it finds ([Validation Errors](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/navigation/map_bundle_format/#validation-errors)) and changes nothing.
- After each upload or settings change, read the SHA-256 again before the next one.

Uploading a bundle replaces all of its settings, including changes saved on the Station page or with the CLI. Copy those changes into your files before you upload a new version.

______________________________________________________________________

## 3. Check the Values for the First Run

A bundle made for another robot needs your robot's values. Check these before the first run:

| Value           | Setting                                                                                                                    | Group in **NAVIGATION SETTINGS** |
| --------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| Robot size      | `robot_radius` of `local_costmap` and `global_costmap` (the same value in both)                                            | Navigator                        |
| Speeds          | `FollowPath.desired_linear_vel` (cruise speed), `FollowPath.max_angular_vel` (turn rate), `velocity_smoother.max_velocity` | Navigator                        |
| Camera mounting | `xyz` and `quat` of the edge from `base_link` to the camera; the height is measured **from the floor**                     | Camera calibration               |
| Camera frame    | `camera_frame_id`: the **frame id** in the camera node's **CAMERA SETTINGS**                                               | Camera calibration               |
| Start pose      | `x`, `y`, `yaw` of `base_link` on the map                                                                                  | Initial pose                     |

### Change Settings

After the upload, the settings in `localizer.yaml`, `navigator.yaml`, `extrinsics.yaml` and `initial_pose.yaml` can be changed without a new bundle:

- **Station page:** select the Localizer or the Navigator node. The inspector's **NAVIGATION SETTINGS** section groups the keys your files contain as Localizer, Navigator, Camera calibration and Initial pose.
- **CLI:** `sodero navigation get --node sodero.navigator`, edit the returned `config`, then `sodero navigation apply` with its SHA-256 (see [sodero CLI](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/ssh_workspace/sodero_cli/index.md)).

Stop the Localizer, the Navigator and Visual odometry before you save; the new values apply when the nodes start again. The map files, `meta.yaml` and `map.file` change only with a new bundle. Every key is described in [Map Bundle Format](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/navigation/map_bundle_format/#files).

______________________________________________________________________

## 4. Start and Set the Initial Pose

1. Start the nodes in this order: the gateway and Strider, the camera gateway (and Visual odometry), the Localizer, the Navigator.
1. Open Strider's **Navigation** page (the **Strider** link on the Navigator's card). **Localization Status** shows **Healthy** once the camera view matches the map.
1. If the status stays **Initializing** or **Lost**, or the robot appears at the wrong place, click **Set Initial Pose**, press on the map where the robot stands and drag in the direction it faces ([Strider › Set the Initial Pose](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/controllers/strider/#set-the-initial-pose)).

The Localizer starts from the bundle's initial pose when it has no confirmed pose on this map. Once it has localized, it restarts from its last confirmed pose on the same `map_id`. A pose set with **Set Initial Pose**, or with the `localization.set_initial_pose` tool, replaces both. Give a changed map a new `map_id` so that an old pose is not reused.

Before you drive a real robot on a new map, check in simulation that the status reaches **Healthy** and that the robot reaches a nearby goal.

______________________________________________________________________

## 5. Troubleshooting

| Symptom or message                                                            | Cause and fix                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| *… the file name must end with .tar.gz or .tgz or .tar or .zip*               | A `.nav` file name on the Station page. Rename the file to `site.nav.tgz`.                                                                                                                           |
| *the localizer is running — stop it before replacing its bundle*              | Stop the Localizer, then upload again.                                                                                                                                                               |
| *Read the current navigation SHA-256 before applying a map.*                  | The SHA-256 is out of date. Run `sodero navigation get` again.                                                                                                                                       |
| The status stays **Initializing**                                             | The camera height in the extrinsics is not measured from the floor, `camera_frame_id` differs from the camera's **frame id**, or the initial pose is far off. Fix the value or set the initial pose. |
| The Localizer log shows `camera_frame_id is required` or `no_extrinsics_edge` | `extrinsics.yaml` has no `camera_frame_id`, or no edge connects the camera's **frame id** to `base_link`.                                                                                            |
| Other messages of the upload                                                  | See [Map Bundle Format › Validation Errors](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/navigation/map_bundle_format/#validation-errors).                                                                |
# Tutorials

# Navigate in Simulation

This tutorial continues the [Quick Start](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/get_started/quick_start/index.md). You add a camera, the Localizer and the Navigator to the simulated Jackal, load the map of its warehouse, let the robot find itself on the map, and send it to a goal.

The Jackal (center) driving to a goal in the warehouse, guided by the Station's navigation stack

______________________________________________________________________

## Before You Start

| You need              | Details                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| --------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The Quick Start setup | `sodero.actuator_gateway.jackal` and `sodero.mlc.jackal`, running, with the Jackal driving in Isaac Sim                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| The example scene     | `jackal_warehouse.usd` from the Quick Start ([jackal_warehouse.zip](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/get_started/quick_start/files/jackal_warehouse.zip)). The Jackal carries a depth camera `cam0` on its `base_link`, 0.22 m ahead of the base and 0.47 m above the floor, looking forward with a 90° horizontal field of view. |
| The map bundle        | [warehouse.nav.tgz](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/navigation/simulation_tutorial/files/warehouse.nav.tgz): the map of the warehouse scene with the settings used in this tutorial                                                                                                                                              |

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 1: Prepare Isaac Sim

The localizer in this tutorial uses the camera at 320 × 240 pixels and 5 frames per second. Isaac Bridge renders cameras at 640 × 480 and 15 frames per second unless told otherwise, so start Isaac Sim from its installation folder with this camera setting (close it first if it runs):

```
RC_ISAAC_CAMERA_DEVICES='[{"name": "cam0", "width": 320, "height": 240, "fps": 5}]' ./isaac-sim.sh
```

```
set "RC_ISAAC_CAMERA_DEVICES=[{"name": "cam0", "width": 320, "height": 240, "fps": 5}]"
isaac-sim.bat
```

Then open `jackal_warehouse.usd` and press **Play**. The Isaac Bridge window lists `cam0 320x240 at 5 fps`.

Check two more things before you go on:

- **Clocks.** The clocks of Stellar X and the Isaac Sim computer must agree within 20 ms. Synchronize both with a time server (NTP). If you cannot, see [Camera Timing](#camera-timing).
- **Quick Start nodes.** If you restarted Isaac Sim for this step, check that the gateway logs *Simulator connected again; turn the servo on to continue.* once the scene plays: the nodes reconnect by themselves ([Connect to Stellar Station › Stop, Pause and Play](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/virtual_simulation/connect_station/#4-stop-pause-and-play)). You switch the servo on again in [Step 6](#step-6-start-and-localize).

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 2: Add the Camera Gateway

1. **Add node** › **Gateway** › **Camera gateway**, name it `cam0` ([Cameras and IMUs](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/gateways/sensors_and_cameras/#1-camera-gateway)).
1. In its inspector, set **Camera name** `cam0` (the camera prim's name in the scene) and **Camera host** (the Isaac Sim computer). The port is `53335`.
1. With the camera node stopped, open **CAMERA SETTINGS** and enter the values of the table below. **horizontal fov deg** is under **Intrinsics**; a new gateway shows it without a mode selector.
1. Click **Save settings**, then **Start node**. Open **Camera view** on its card and check that frames arrive at `320 × 240`, about `5 fps`. If the image stays empty, see [Camera Timing](#camera-timing).

Change the camera defaults before localization

A new camera gateway starts with **horizontal fov deg = 60** and **fps = 15**. The Jackal camera in `jackal_warehouse.usd` has a **90°** horizontal field of view, and this tutorial uses **5 fps**. Change both values before starting the Localizer. A visible image confirms reception; it does not confirm correct camera calibration. A wrong field of view distorts the 3D points reconstructed from depth, so the Localizer can remain **Initializing**, **Relocalizing** or **Lost** even while the image looks normal.

| Setting in CAMERA SETTINGS                 | New gateway default | Value for this tutorial                                |
| ------------------------------------------ | ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Intrinsics › horizontal fov deg**        | `60`                | **`90` — change this**                                 |
| **General › fps**                          | `15`                | **`5` — change this**                                  |
| **General › frame id**                     | `cam0_optical`      | `cam0_optical`                                         |
| **General › width**, **height**            | `0`, `0`            | Keep `0`, `0`: detect `320 × 240` from incoming frames |
| **Simulation camera › capture latency ns** | `0`                 | Keep `0` for this example                              |
| **Simulation camera › recv timeout ms**    | `1000`              | Keep `1000`                                            |

The gateway's **fps** setting does not change Isaac Sim's rendering rate. Set the source to `320 × 240` at `5 fps` in [Step 1](#step-1-prepare-isaac-sim). For a different scene or camera, enter its actual field of view; `90` is the value for this example. Isaac Bridge prints the field of view when the scene starts.

The Jackal's camera

If you already started navigation with the defaults, see [Correct Settings on a Running Setup](#correct-settings-on-a-running-setup).

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 3: Add the Localizer and Load the Map

1. **Add node** › **Controller** › **Localizer**. It is named `sodero.localizer`.
1. In its inspector, click **Upload .nav** and choose `warehouse.nav.tgz`. The inspector shows the map: `warehouse · 500×620 @ 0.05 m`, and the initial pose of the bundle.

The localizer with its map and connections

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 4: Add the Navigator

**Add node** › **Controller** › **Navigator**. It is named `sodero.navigator` and uses the navigator settings of the same map bundle.

The navigator, using the same map bundle

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 5: Connect the Ports

Drag these five connections (from the required port on the left of a card to the provided port on the right of another):

| From                                | To                                      |
| ----------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| `sodero.localizer` › `camera`       | `sodero.camera_gateway.cam0` › `camera` |
| `sodero.localizer` › `odometry`     | `sodero.mlc.jackal` › `odometry`        |
| `sodero.navigator` › `localization` | `sodero.localizer` › `localization`     |
| `sodero.navigator` › `map`          | `sodero.localizer` › `map`              |
| `sodero.navigator` › `mobile_base`  | `sodero.mlc.jackal` › `mobile_base`     |

The complete navigation graph, all nodes operating

When the Station has several Strider nodes, make sure the localizer's `odometry` and the navigator's `mobile_base` connect to the **same** robot.

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 6: Start and Localize

1. In Isaac Sim, stop and play the scene so the Jackal is back at its starting pose.
1. Start the nodes in order: `sodero.localizer`, then `sodero.navigator` (the gateway, the Strider and the camera already run).
1. In the gateway's log, after *Simulator connected again*, open Strider and switch **Twist** and **Servo On** again (a simulation restart turns the servo off).
1. Open Strider's **Navigation** page (the **Strider** link on the Navigator's card). **Localization Status** shows **Healthy** once the camera view matches the map.

If the status stays **Initializing**, **Relocalizing** or **Lost** while the camera image is visible, first check the saved **horizontal fov deg = 90** and **fps = 5** settings from [Step 2](#step-2-add-the-camera-gateway). If they are correct and the robot still cannot localize or appears at the wrong place, set the initial pose: click **Set Initial Pose** ①, press on the map where the robot is and drag in the direction it faces ②, then click **Set initial pose** (**Relocalize here** ③ when a pose was set before).

Setting the initial pose

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 7: Send a Goal

1. Click **Set Goal**, press on the map at the goal and drag in the direction the robot should face. **Goal Pose** shows the coordinates.

   The goal is set; the robot is localized (Healthy)

1. Click **Start Navigation**. The planned path appears and the robot drives; **Navigator** shows *following* and **Route Summary** the remaining distance.

Following the path to the goal

When the robot arrives, **Recent Goals** shows *Reached* and **Navigation Events** *Navigation idle: reached*.

Goal reached

The Jackal at the goal in Isaac Sim

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 8: Finish

Click **Cancel** if a goal is still running, switch the servo off and choose **Idle** in Strider, then stop the nodes (navigator, localizer, camera, Strider, gateway) and the Isaac Sim scene.

______________________________________________________________________

## Troubleshooting

### Camera Timing

Every camera frame carries its capture time on the Isaac Sim computer's clock, and the camera gateway accepts only frames captured at most 20 ms ahead of and 2 s behind Stellar X's clock. It drops the others: the **Camera view** in Step 2 stays empty, and the camera gateway's log shows *Frames … are stale or carry capture times that do not match this Station's clock (clock skew?)*. Two computers that each follow a time server on the internet are easily more than 20 ms apart.

If you cannot synchronize the clocks, start Isaac Sim with `RC_CAMERA_CAPTURE_TIME=0` as well. The frames then carry no capture time, and the camera gateway stamps each frame when it arrives. An arrival time is later than the capture time by the rendering and network delay, so synchronized clocks remain the better choice for localization.

```
RC_CAMERA_CAPTURE_TIME=0 RC_ISAAC_CAMERA_DEVICES='[{"name": "cam0", "width": 320, "height": 240, "fps": 5}]' ./isaac-sim.sh
```

```
set "RC_CAMERA_CAPTURE_TIME=0"
set "RC_ISAAC_CAMERA_DEVICES=[{"name": "cam0", "width": 320, "height": 240, "fps": 5}]"
isaac-sim.bat
```

### Nodes After an Isaac Sim Restart

Restarting Isaac Sim interrupts the robot: the gateway loses the simulator and switches the servo off, and Strider stops the base. The nodes reconnect by themselves. Once the scene plays again, wait until the gateway logs *Simulator connected again; turn the servo on to continue.*, then switch **Twist** and **Servo On** again in Strider ([Connect to Stellar Station › Stop, Pause and Play](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/virtual_simulation/connect_station/#4-stop-pause-and-play)). The Localizer may still hold its last pose; set the initial pose again if the robot appears at the wrong place.

### Correct Settings on a Running Setup

If you already started navigation with the defaults:

1. Cancel any active navigation goal and wait for the robot to stop.
1. Stop **Navigator → Localizer → Camera gateway**. The camera settings become editable after the camera node stops.
1. Set **horizontal fov deg** to `90` and **fps** to `5`, then click **Save settings**.
1. Start **Camera gateway → Localizer → Navigator**. Check the camera image and wait for **Localization Status: Healthy**. If it still needs an initial pose, set the robot's actual position and direction as described in [Step 6](#step-6-start-and-localize).

______________________________________________________________________

## Tips for Your Own Robot

- **Run the simulation in real time.** The controllers follow the simulation's time, but the camera localization runs on wall time. A slow simulation makes localization lag behind.
- **Skid-steer bases turn less than their wheels say**, because the wheels slide sideways. Let the robot turn in place before it drives (`rotate_to_heading_min_angle` about 0.25 rad), and calibrate the wheel offsets of the `.sddm` so odometry matches the real turn.
- **Repeating structures** (identical racks, long corridors) can mislead the localizer. Limit the correction per update (`icp.max_jump_m`, `icp.max_jump_rad`) and keep distinct objects in the camera's view.
- **The camera height** in the map bundle's extrinsics is measured from the floor ([Localization and Navigation](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/navigation/overview/#2-coordinate-frames)).

______________________________________________________________________

Next: [Create a Map from Your Site](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/navigation/create_map/index.md), for the map of your own site.

# EtherCAT Mobile Base

This tutorial drives a four-wheel skid-steer base with four EtherCAT servo drives from Stellar X. It is the [Quick Start](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/get_started/quick_start/index.md) system on real motors: Strider still drives the base, and an EtherCAT gateway takes the place of the simulation gateway. You will:

1. wire the four drives to Stellar X,
1. add the gateway and Strider on Stellar Station and load their example documents,
1. bring up the EtherCAT network,
1. turn each wheel on its own from the gateway's test console, and
1. jog the wheels with Strider.

```
flowchart TB
    B["Your browser<br>Stellar Station · Strider"]
    subgraph SX ["Stellar X"]
        S["Strider<br>sodero.mlc.base"] -- servo_link --> G["EtherCAT gateway<br>sodero.actuator_gateway.wheels"]
    end
    subgraph EC ["EtherCAT line"]
        direction LR
        D1["Drive 1<br>front left"] --> D2["Drive 2<br>front right"] --> D3["Drive 3<br>rear left"] --> D4["Drive 4<br>rear right"]
    end
    B --> S
    G -- "EtherCAT Out" --> EC
```

**Real motors move.** Lift the base so that its wheels are off the ground until every wheel turns the right way. Wire the drives' safe torque off (STO) and an emergency stop, and keep the emergency stop within reach ([Stop Controls](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/hardware_setup/stop_controls/index.md)).

______________________________________________________________________

## Before You Start

| You need          | Details                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| ----------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Stellar X         | Powered on and reachable from your PC ([Network Settings](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/hardware_setup/stellar_series/network_settings/index.md)). In this guide its address is `192.168.60.18`.                                                 |
| Four servo drives | EtherCAT drives with the CiA 402 profile and cyclic synchronous velocity (CSV). Their RxPDO must include **Target velocity (0x60FF)** ([EtherCAT Gateway › What You Need](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/gateways/ethercat/#1-what-you-need)).    |
| Motors            | One motor per wheel. The example uses motors with a rated torque of 2.2222 Nm, a peak torque of 6.6667 Nm, a maximum speed of 1,890 rpm and an encoder with 524,288 counts per turn, each behind a 7.75 : 1 gear.                                          |
| A four-wheel base | The example base has wheels of 0.098 m radius at ±0.131 m front and back and ±0.188 m left and right of the base center.                                                                                                                                   |
| Example files     | [wheels.gw](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/tutorials/ethercat_mobile_base/files/wheels.gw) (EtherCAT gateway with four drives) and [base.sddm](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/tutorials/ethercat_mobile_base/files/base.sddm) (Strider). |

Your drives, motors and base are probably not the example's. Load the example files anyway and change the values in the Gateway Designer and Stellar Designer, as the steps below describe.

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 1: Wire the Drives

1. Plug Stellar X's **EtherCAT Out** port into the **IN** port of the front-left drive.
1. Connect its **OUT** port to the **IN** port of the front-right drive, then on to the rear-left and the rear-right drive.
1. Power the drives and release their STO and the emergency stop.

The cable order is the actuator order of the gateway, and the Strider document assigns the actuators to the wheels:

| Drive on the cable | Gateway actuator | Wheel             |
| ------------------ | ---------------- | ----------------- |
| 1st                | 1 (index 0)      | `fl`, front left  |
| 2nd                | 2 (index 1)      | `fr`, front right |
| 3rd                | 3 (index 2)      | `rl`, rear left   |
| 4th                | 4 (index 3)      | `rr`, rear right  |

Do not use a network switch. EtherCAT frames must pass through the drives in a line ([EtherCAT Gateway › Wire the Drives](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/gateways/ethercat/#2-wire-the-drives)).

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 2: Add the Gateway and Load `wheels.gw`

1. Open `http://192.168.60.18` in your browser.

1. Click **Add node**, choose **Gateway** › **Actuator gateway** and click **Next**. Name it `wheels` and click **Add node** ([Quick Start › Step 1](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/get_started/quick_start/#step-1-add-the-gateway)).

1. Select `sodero.actuator_gateway.wheels`. In its inspector, click the upload icon in **DEFINITION** (**Import .gw**), choose `wheels.gw` on **From your PC** and click **Import**.

1. Click **Edit Stellar Gateway Designer** to check the document.

   ① four actuators, one per drive in cable order ② the Motor tab of actuator 1

   The gateway has four actuators ①, one per drive. Every actuator has the same **Motor** tab ②:

   | Field              | Example value |
   | ------------------ | ------------- |
   | **Rated torque**   | 2.2222 Nm     |
   | **Max torque**     | 6.6667 Nm     |
   | **Max speed**      | 1,890 rpm     |
   | **Resolution**     | 524,288 PPR   |
   | **Encoder offset** | 0 pulse       |
   | **Gear ratio**     | 7.75          |

   The **EtherCAT** tab of each actuator holds the drive's position on the cable (**Idx** 0 to 3), its label (`drive_fl` to `drive_rr`) and the PDO mapping: the six RxPDO and the six TxPDO objects listed in [Process Data](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/gateways/ethercat/#process-data), including **Target velocity (0x60FF)**.

1. If your hardware differs, change it here: select your drive in the **EtherCAT** tab and enter your motor in the **Motor** tab of each actuator ([EtherCAT Gateway › Create the Gateway Document](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/gateways/ethercat/#3-create-the-gateway-document)).

1. Open **02 Verification**, click **Verify** and fix any errors. Then click the back arrow to return to the Station.

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 3: Add Strider and Connect It

1. Click **Add node**, choose **Controller** › **Strider** and click **Next**. Name it `base` and click **Add node**.
1. Select `sodero.mlc.base`, click the upload icon in **DEFINITION** (**Import .sddm**), choose `base.sddm` and click **Import**.
1. Connect the two nodes: drag from the Strider's `servo_link` to the gateway's `servo_link`, or click **Auto-connect** next to `servo_link` in the Strider's inspector.

① the gateway and Strider connected through servo_link ② the gateway's document ③ the gateway's log after a start

`base.sddm` describes the example base: a skid-steer chassis with four drive wheels, 0.098 m wheel radius and 17 kg. For your own base, select `sodero.mlc.base`, click **Edit Stellar Designer** and enter its dimensions and limits ([Mobile Robot (.sddm)](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/tutorials/stellar_designer/mobile_robot/index.md)).

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 4: Start the Gateway

1. Select the gateway and click **Start node**. Wait until its state is **Operating**.

1. In its **LOGS** (stream **Gateway events**) ③, check that all four drives answered and reached operation:

   ```
   Gateway sodero.actuator_gateway.wheels starting: EtherCAT, 4 actuator(s), 1.0 ms cycle.
   EtherCAT: starting on network port 'eth0' (4 drive(s) expected).
   EtherCAT: found drive 1 (…).
   EtherCAT: found drive 2 (…).
   EtherCAT: found drive 3 (…).
   EtherCAT: found drive 4 (…).
   EtherCAT ready: 4 drive(s) operational, 1.0 ms cycle.
   ```

   Each *found drive* line names the drive as the drive reports itself.

If the gateway stops before *EtherCAT ready*, its log says why: no cable link, a drive missing from the chain, a PDO mapping that does not match the drive, or a drive that refuses the configuration. See [EtherCAT Gateway › Troubleshooting](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/gateways/ethercat/#6-troubleshooting).

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 5: Test the Wheels with the Test Console

Check every wheel with the gateway's [test console](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/gateways/test_console/index.md) before Strider drives them. That page describes the console and how to open and end a test; this step gives the values for the four wheels.

1. Select the gateway and click **Test Stellar Gateway** in its **CONTROL** section. The test console opens in a new browser tab. While the test runs, the graph shows it as `sodero.actuator_test.wheels` ①, and the gateway's **CONTROL** section shows **Open test console** and **Stop test** ②.

   ① the test console, connected to the gateway's servo_link ② the gateway's test console buttons

1. In the console, check that the top bar shows **Gateway Connected** and that there are four cards, **A1** to **A4**. Card **A1** is actuator 1, the first drive on the cable.

   ① EMERGENCY STOP ② Servo ON and Servo OFF ③ the drive mode of all actuators ④ the target velocity of actuator 1

1. Under **DRIVE MODE — APPLY TO ALL AXES** ③, choose **VELOCITY** and click **Apply**.

1. Click **Servo ON** ②. Check the gateway's log on the Station page for *Servo ON: all 4 drive(s) enabled.*

1. On card **A1**, press and hold the **dqa_d · Target Velocity** slider ④ and drag it to the right, to about 60 deg/s. The wheel turns while you hold the mouse button and stops when you release it. Keep the console's tab open while a wheel turns.

1. Do the same on cards **A2**, **A3** and **A4**.

Each card must turn its own wheel ([Step 1](#step-1-wire-the-drives)) forward, the way the base drives forward. At 60 deg/s a wheel needs 6 s for one turn.

| What you see                                 | Cause and fix                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| -------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| A different wheel turns                      | The cable order does not match the wheel order. Rewire the drives in the order of [Step 1](#step-1-wire-the-drives).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| The wheel turns backward                     | The motor is mounted the other way round. Invert its direction in the drive, for example with the drive's polarity parameter as a start-up SDO in the **EtherCAT** tab. Leave the influence factor in the Strider document at `1` ([Mobile Robot › Actuator Mapping](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/tutorials/stellar_designer/mobile_robot/#step-3-actuator-mapping)). |
| One turn takes clearly more or less than 6 s | **Gear ratio** or **Resolution** in the gateway is wrong.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |

Other problems, such as a drive that does not enable, are in [Test Console › Troubleshooting](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/gateways/test_console/#troubleshooting). To change the gateway document, for example a drive's polarity, end the test first ([Test Console › Change the Gateway Document](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/gateways/test_console/#change-the-gateway-document)).

When every wheel passes, click **Servo OFF** in the console, then **Stop test** in the gateway's **CONTROL** section ([Test Console › End the Test](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/gateways/test_console/#end-the-test)).

______________________________________________________________________

## Step 6: Jog the Wheels with Strider

1. Select the Strider and click **Start node**. The gateway's log shows *Robot controller connected.*
1. In the Strider's inspector, click **Strider** in **CONTROL** and open the **Drive** page ([Strider › Jog the Base](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/controllers/strider/#4-jog-the-base-drive-page)).
1. Under **Drive Mode**, click **Twist**. Under **Servo / Safety**, switch **Servo On**. The gateway's log shows *Servo ON: all 4 drive(s) enabled.*
1. Set **Linear Velocity Limit** to a low value, such as 0.1 m/s.
1. Press and hold **Forward (W)** for a moment. All four wheels turn forward.
1. Press and hold **Turn Left (A)**. The left wheels turn backward and the right wheels forward.

The wheels passed the test console, so a wrong wheel or direction here comes from the Strider document: its actuator mapping must assign actuators 1 to 4 to `fl`, `fr`, `rl` and `rr`, each with the influence factor `1` ([Mobile Robot › Actuator Mapping](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/tutorials/stellar_designer/mobile_robot/#step-3-actuator-mapping)). If the wheels turn too fast or too slow, check the wheel radius in the Strider document.

When every wheel turns the right way, switch the servo off and click **Idle**. Put the base on the ground and drive it slowly, with the limits still low.

______________________________________________________________________

## What's Next

| Next step                                                  | Page                                                                                                             |
| ---------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Every Strider control, odometry calibration and programs   | [Strider](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/controllers/strider/index.md)                                  |
| Localize the base on a map and drive it to goals           | [Localization and Navigation](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/navigation/overview/index.md)              |

# Extend and Automate

# SSH Workspace

Stellar X includes a development workspace that you reach over SSH. It runs on the controller itself, next to Stellar Station but separated from real-time control. It still shares the controller's memory and storage, so avoid very large builds while the robot is moving.

From the workspace you can:

- inspect and change the Station with the `sodero` command-line tool: nodes, connections, design documents, settings, maps and packages;
- read the status and logs of every node, as the Station page shows them, and call robot tools such as Strider, Motion Studio and navigation;
- write and test your own programs and install them on the Station as modules;
- let an AI coding agent do all of the above for you (see [AI Coding Agents](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/ssh_workspace/ai_agents/index.md)).

The workspace performs the same operations as the Station page: a node added with `sodero topology add-node` is the same node you would add with **Add node**.

______________________________________________________________________

## 1. Register Your SSH Key

The workspace accepts SSH keys only; there is no password sign-in. Register the public key of every computer that should connect, in the **SSH ACCESS** card of the robot's Network Settings page (`http://ROBOT_ADDRESS:3000`): copy the key command for your operating system, run it on your computer, paste the line it prints and click **Add key**. The steps and the commands are in [Network Settings › SSH Access](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/hardware_setup/stellar_series/network_settings/#2-ssh-access).

To revoke a computer's access, click the trash icon next to its key on the same page.

______________________________________________________________________

## 2. Connect

The **SSH workspace** card on the Network Settings page shows the command with a **Copy** button:

```
ssh -p 2222 sodero@192.168.60.18
```

Replace the address with your robot's address. The user name is always `sodero` and the port is always `2222`.

**Tip:** Save a host alias

Add this to `~/.ssh/config` on your computer, so that `ssh stellar-x` is enough:

```
Host stellar-x
    HostName 192.168.60.18
    Port 2222
    User sodero
```

Check where you are before you change anything:

```
sodero project status
sodero runtime status
```

Stellar X has a single Station, with the ID `station`. Every command uses it by default, so you never need `--item`.

______________________________________________________________________

## 3. What Is in the Workspace

| Path                   | Contents                                                                                                                            |
| ---------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `/workspace`           | Your files. They stay on the robot across restarts and software updates.                                                            |
| `/workspace/README.md` | The workspace guide: terms, a five-minute start and the guide map                                                                   |
| `/workspace/AGENTS.md` | Operating rules for AI coding agents ([AI Coding Agents](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/ssh_workspace/ai_agents/index.md)) |
| `/opt/sodero/docs/`    | All workspace guides and examples, read-only. Also linked as `/workspace/docs`.                                                     |

| Tool                                | Purpose                                                                                                             |
| ----------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `sodero`                            | Station command-line tool ([sodero CLI](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/ssh_workspace/sodero_cli/index.md)) |
| `sodero-help`                       | Prints the guides: `sodero-help` lists them, `sodero-help navigation` opens one                                     |
| Python 3.12                         | With numpy, PyYAML, requests, aiohttp and onnxruntime                                                               |
| `git`, `gcc`, `make`, `scp`, `sftp` | Standard development tools                                                                                          |

The robot's workspace has **no Internet access**. Copy the dependencies your code needs from your computer (for example as wheel files) with `scp`.

______________________________________________________________________

## 4. Copy Files

Use `scp` or any SFTP client with the same address, user and port:

```
# Once: create a folder for your work on the robot
ssh -p 2222 sodero@192.168.60.18 mkdir -p /workspace/my-work

# From your computer to the robot
scp -P 2222 my_robot.gw sodero@192.168.60.18:/workspace/my-work/

# From the robot to your computer
scp -P 2222 sodero@192.168.60.18:/workspace/my-work/result.json .
```

______________________________________________________________________

## 5. Use VS Code

VS Code's **Remote - SSH** extension connects with the same command.

1. In VS Code settings, set `remote.SSH.localServerDownload` to `always`. The robot has no Internet access, so VS Code copies its server from your computer.
1. Run **Remote-SSH: Add New SSH Host...** from the Command Palette and enter `ssh -p 2222 sodero@192.168.60.18`.
1. Run **Remote-SSH: Connect to Host...**, choose the robot's address and open the folder `/workspace`.

The first connection copies the VS Code server (about 230 MB) and takes a minute or two. Later connections take seconds.

______________________________________________________________________

## 6. Rules of the Road

- **Preview first.** A `sodero` command that changes something only previews until you add `--execute`. Read the preview, then repeat the command with `--execute`.
- **The robot is real equipment.** A command with `--execute` can start nodes or move the robot. Run it only when the surroundings are clear and someone who can stop the robot is present.
- **Stop a node before you change it.** The Station refuses changes to a running node. Stop it, apply the change, start it again.

Where to go next:

| Task                                                           | Where                                                                                                       |
| -------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Command reference and examples                                 | [sodero CLI](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/ssh_workspace/sodero_cli/index.md)                     |
| Let an AI agent work on the robot                              | [AI Coding Agents](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/ssh_workspace/ai_agents/index.md)                |
| Load a whole design document (`.gw`, `.sdd`, `.sddm`, `.sdda`) | Station page: [Design Documents](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/station/design_documents/index.md) |
| Write your own module                                          | [Create Custom Modules](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/extend/custom_modules/index.md)             |

# sodero CLI

`sodero` is the command-line tool of the SSH workspace. It performs the operations of the Station page (adding nodes, connecting ports, loading settings and maps, starting nodes, calling robot tools) and prints every result as JSON, so people, scripts and AI agents can all use it.

The CLI is its own best reference:

| Command                                            | What it gives                                                |
| -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `sodero --help`                                    | All command groups                                           |
| `sodero GROUP ACTION --help`                       | Every option of one command, with defaults                   |
| `sodero capabilities`                              | The full command list, exit codes and limits as JSON         |
| `sodero tools list` / `sodero tools describe TOOL` | The robot tools of the running nodes and their input schemas |
| `sodero-help` / `sodero-help NAME`                 | The workspace guides, for example `sodero-help navigation`   |

______________________________________________________________________

## Conventions

- **JSON output.** Each command prints one JSON result on stdout. Pipe it through `python3 -m json.tool` to read it comfortably. A failure prints one JSON error on stderr: `{"error": {"code": ..., "message": ..., "details": ...}}`.
- **Preview first.** A command that changes something only previews until you add `--execute`. Read the preview, then repeat the command with `--execute`.
- **Versions.** Changes to the node graph take `--if-version N`, the `expected_version` from `sodero topology get`. Changes to settings and documents take `--if-sha256 SHA256` from the matching `get`. Each saved change returns the next value. If someone changed the Station page in the meantime, the change is refused with a conflict (exit code 6): read again and retry.
- **One Station.** On a robot, the only item is the Station `station`. `--item` defaults to it and can be left out.
- **Node IDs.** A node's ID comes from its module, not from the `--kind` option of `topology add-node`: `--kind camera --name cam0` creates `sodero.camera_gateway.cam0`, and `--kind strider --name jackal` creates `sodero.mlc.jackal`. The IDs of all built-in modules are listed in [Key Concepts › Station and Nodes](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/get_started/key_concepts/#station-and-nodes).

### Exit Codes

| Code | Meaning                      | What to do                                            |
| ---- | ---------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| 0    | Success                      | For an accepted change, check the returned state      |
| 1    | Other failure                | Read `error.message` and fix the cause                |
| 2    | Invalid arguments            | Check `--help`                                        |
| 3    | Authentication or permission | Reconnect; ask the robot's operator                   |
| 4    | Service unavailable          | Check the state before you repeat a change            |
| 5    | Timeout                      | Check the state; run the printed resume command       |
| 6    | Conflict                     | Read the current version or SHA-256 again, then retry |
| 7    | Busy                         | Retry after a pause                                   |
| 8    | Limit exceeded               | Reduce the size or count                              |

______________________________________________________________________

## Command Map

| Group                    | Actions                                                                        | Use                                                                        |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `project`                | `status`                                                                       | Station and workspace information                                          |
| `runtime`                | `status`, `logs`, `start`, `stop`, `node start`, `node stop`                   | Which nodes run, their logs; start and stop nodes                          |
| `topology`               | `catalog`, `get`, `add-node`, `connect`, `disconnect`, `remove-node`, `import` | Edit the node graph                                                        |
| `tools`                  | `list`, `describe`, `call`                                                     | Robot tools: Strider, Motion Studio, navigation, localization, documents…  |
| `navigation`             | `list`, `get`, `apply`                                                         | Settings of the camera, visual odometry, localizer and navigator           |
| `maps`                   | `upload`, `attach`                                                             | Attach `.nav` map bundles to the localizer and navigator                   |
| `locomotion`, `policies` | `list`, `get`, `apply`; `upload`                                               | Legged locomotion and IMU settings; your own ONNX walking policy           |
| `articulations`          | `get`, `configure`, `upload`                                                   | Joints and actuators of Articulation nodes                                 |
| `packages`               | `list`, `upload`, `remove`                                                     | Your own modules                                                           |
| `apps`                   | `start`, `stop`, `status`, `logs`, `call`                                      | Nodes of your own modules                                                  |
| `watch`, `camera`        | `watch`; `camera snapshot`                                                     | Sample readings for a few seconds; save a camera picture                   |
| `files`                  | `upload`                                                                       | Stage a file on the robot for `documents.apply` (kept for at most 6 hours) |
| `run`, `programs`        | `run`; `programs list`, `programs logs`                                        | Run a program in the workspace and keep its output                         |

Worlds, project items, the project Library and Sodero Assets belong to Sodero Cloud. On a robot these commands answer `NOT_AVAILABLE_ON_DEVICE`.

______________________________________________________________________

## Recipes

### Status and Logs

```
sodero runtime status                                    # every node: configured, running, its state
sodero runtime logs sodero.actuator_gateway.jackal --lines 100
sodero tools call strider.get_state --input '{"target":"sodero.mlc.jackal"}'
```

### Start and Stop Nodes

```
sodero runtime node start sodero.actuator_gateway.jackal --execute   # gateway first
sodero runtime node start sodero.mlc.jackal --execute                # then its controller
sodero runtime node stop sodero.mlc.jackal --execute
```

`sodero runtime start --execute --wait` starts every saved node, like **Start all nodes** on the Station page.

**Start all nodes** includes nodes that drive real hardware. Start nodes one by one when the graph contains hardware you do not want to run.

### Edit the Node Graph

Stop the nodes you change first, as on the Station page; changes apply when they next start. Every graph change needs the current version. Read it, preview, then execute:

```
sodero topology get                                       # note "expected_version", e.g. 12
sodero topology add-node --kind camera --name cam0 --if-version 12              # preview
sodero topology add-node --kind camera --name cam0 --if-version 12 --execute    # returns version 13
sodero topology connect --source sodero.localizer.camera \
    --target sodero.camera_gateway.cam0.camera --if-version 13 --execute
```

`sodero topology catalog` lists the node kinds with their ports: `gateway`, `strider`, `motion_studio`, `articulation`, `camera`, `imu`, `vo`, `localizer`, `navigator` and `package`. For legged robots, which are prepared with Sodero support, it also lists `legged_locomotion` and `legged_navigator`, a navigator that drives a Legged locomotion node.

### Change Settings of Built-in Nodes

```
sodero navigation list
sodero navigation get --node sodero.navigator > navigator.json   # the editable config and its sha256
# save the "config" part to config.json and change the values you need, then:
sodero navigation apply --node sodero.navigator --config @config.json --if-sha256 SHA256            # preview
sodero navigation apply --node sodero.navigator --config @config.json --if-sha256 SHA256 --execute
```

Stop the node first; the new settings apply when it starts again. These are the same settings the Station page shows in the node's inspector.

### Attach a Map

```
sodero runtime node stop sodero.navigator --execute          # stop the nodes that use the map
sodero runtime node stop sodero.localizer --execute
sodero runtime node stop sodero.visual_odometry --execute    # if the Station has one
sodero navigation get --node sodero.localizer                # note "sha256"
sodero maps upload /workspace/maps/warehouse.nav --node sodero.localizer --if-sha256 SHA256            # preview: checks the bundle
sodero maps upload /workspace/maps/warehouse.nav --node sodero.localizer --if-sha256 SHA256 --execute  # attach it
```

The localizer and the navigator share one map bundle, so one upload serves both. Start the nodes again afterwards. See [Load and Configure a Map](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/navigation/map_bundle/index.md) and [Localization and Navigation](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/navigation/overview/index.md).

### Modules (Your Own Programs)

```
sodero packages upload /workspace/my-work/patrol.tar.gz --execute
sodero topology add-node --kind package --package customer.patrol --if-version N --execute   # name from package.yaml
sodero apps start NODE --execute
sodero apps logs NODE --lines 100
```

See [Create Custom Modules](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/extend/custom_modules/index.md) for the package format.

### Robot Tools

```
sodero tools list                                        # tools of the running nodes, with their targets
sodero tools describe localization.set_initial_pose      # input schema
sodero tools call localization.set_initial_pose --input '{"x": -1.6, "y": 2.4, "yaw": 0.0}'            # preview
sodero tools call localization.set_initial_pose --input '{"x": -1.6, "y": 2.4, "yaw": 0.0}' --execute
```

A tool that changes something or moves the robot acts only with `--execute`. Strider and Motion Studio tools need the exact `target` (from `tools list`) when the Station has more than one robot of that kind, for example `{"mode": "TWIST", "target": "sodero.mlc.jackal"}` for `strider.set_mode`.

### Readings and Pictures

```
sodero watch --probe sodero.mlc.jackal --hz 5 --seconds 5
sodero camera snapshot sodero.camera_gateway.cam0 --output frame.png
```

# AI Coding Agents

The SSH workspace is built for people and AI coding agents alike. Every `sodero` command prints JSON, every change is previewed before it is applied, and the workspace ships its own operating rules for agents. With an agent such as **Claude Code** or **OpenAI Codex**, you describe a task in plain language and the agent runs the commands, reads the results and reports back:

- *"Which nodes are running, and why did the Strider node stop?"*
- *"Add a camera gateway named cam0 and connect it to the localizer."*
- *"Lower the navigator's top speed to 0.3 m/s."*
- *"Write a module that drives the robot through these three waypoints."*

```
flowchart TB
    You(["You"]) --> Agent["AI coding agent<br>on your computer"]
    Agent -- "ssh stellar-x 'sodero …'" --> WS["SSH workspace<br>on Stellar X"]
    WS -- "sodero CLI" --> Station["Stellar Station"]
    Station --> Nodes["Nodes:<br>gateways, controllers,<br>navigation, modules"]
```

The robot's workspace has **no Internet access**, and an AI agent needs the Internet to reach its language model. So the agent runs **on your computer** and works on the robot through SSH: it sends each command with `ssh`, reads the JSON that comes back and decides the next step.

The agent changes the robot only through `sodero`, which performs exactly the operations of the Station page. Whatever the agent builds, you can inspect and change on the Station page, and the other way round.

______________________________________________________________________

## 1. Prepare SSH Access

1. Register your computer's SSH key on the robot's [Network Settings](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/hardware_setup/stellar_series/network_settings/#2-ssh-access) page.

1. Add a host alias to `~/.ssh/config` on your computer, so the agent can use a short name:

   ```
   Host stellar-x
       HostName 192.168.60.18
       Port 2222
       User sodero
   ```

1. Check that a command runs without a prompt:

   ```
   ssh stellar-x sodero project status
   ```

   The first time, SSH asks you to confirm the robot's host key: answer `yes`. After that the command must run without any prompt. It prints one line of JSON that describes the robot's Station.

**Tip (macOS · Linux):** Reuse one SSH connection

Agents run many short commands. Reusing one SSH connection makes each call faster. Add these lines under `Host stellar-x`:

```
    ControlMaster auto
    ControlPath ~/.ssh/cm-%r@%h-%p
    ControlPersist 10m
```

______________________________________________________________________

## 2. Tell the Agent About the Robot

Create a working folder on your computer with an instructions file that your agent reads automatically when it starts: **`CLAUDE.md`** for Claude Code, **`AGENTS.md`** for Codex and most other agents. Copy this text into it:

```
# Stellar X robot

The robot's SSH workspace is reachable as `ssh stellar-x '<command>'`.

Before you change anything, read the robot's own rules and follow them:
`ssh stellar-x cat /workspace/AGENTS.md`

- Use the `sodero` CLI over SSH. It prints JSON; read `sodero --help` and
  `sodero capabilities` instead of guessing commands.
- Commands that change something only preview until `--execute` is added.
  Show me the preview and wait for my OK before you add `--execute`.
- Never move the real robot unless I ask for that motion.
- Keep source files on the robot under /workspace/my-work
  (create it with `mkdir -p /workspace/my-work` if it does not exist).
```

The robot's own rules (`/workspace/AGENTS.md`) tell the agent how to read results and exit codes, how to wait for long operations without polling loops, which nodes drive real hardware on this robot, and what it must never do. They are maintained with the robot's software, so you do not need to copy them.

These rules are instructions to the agent, not a safety function. An agent can misread them or make mistakes, and the `sodero` commands it runs have the same effect as your own clicks on the Station page. Approve every command that changes the robot yourself, and keep the robot's stop controls and the hardware emergency stop ready ([Stop Controls](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/hardware_setup/stop_controls/index.md)).

______________________________________________________________________

## 3. Start the Agent

```
mkdir -p ~/stellar-x-work && cd ~/stellar-x-work
# save the text above as CLAUDE.md
claude
```

```
mkdir -p ~/stellar-x-work && cd ~/stellar-x-work
# save the text above as AGENTS.md
codex
```

Open the folder `~/stellar-x-work` in VS Code and start your agent extension there (for example Claude Code or Codex). The agent runs on your computer and reaches the robot with `ssh stellar-x`.

Start with a read-only request to see that everything is connected:

```
Check the robot's Station and tell me which nodes exist and which are running.
```

The agent runs commands such as `sodero topology get` and `sodero runtime status` and summarizes the result.

______________________________________________________________________

## 4. Example Tasks

| You ask                                                         | What the agent does                                                                                                                                                                      |
| --------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| *"Why did the Strider node fail?"*                              | `sodero runtime status` to find the failed node and its reason, then `sodero runtime logs NODE`                                                                                          |
| *"Add a camera gateway cam0 and connect it to the localizer."*  | `sodero topology get`, then `sodero topology add-node` and `sodero topology connect`, each previewed first                                                                               |
| *"Lower the navigator's maximum speed to 0.3 m/s."*             | `sodero navigation get --node sodero.navigator`, edits the value, `sodero navigation apply` with the returned SHA-256                                                                    |
| *"Attach warehouse.nav to the localizer and the navigator."*    | `sodero navigation get --node sodero.localizer` for its SHA-256, then `sodero maps upload warehouse.nav --node sodero.localizer` with it, previewed first (one upload serves both nodes) |
| *"Write a module that drives to these three points in a loop."* | Writes a package under `/workspace/my-work`, checks it, `sodero packages upload`, adds its node and starts it with `sodero apps start`                                                   |
| *"Drive the simulated robot forward 1 m."*                      | `sodero tools call strider.set_mode`, `strider.servo_on`, `strider.set_twist` and `strider.stop` on the **simulated** robot's target                                                     |

______________________________________________________________________

## 5. Stay in Control

- **Review previews.** Ask the agent to show the preview of every change. Nothing changes until a command runs with `--execute`.
- **Set approval rules in your agent.** Most agents can require your approval before they run a command. A practical setup: allow read-only commands (`status`, `get`, `list`, `logs`) freely, and ask for approval for anything with `--execute`, `tools call` or `apps call`.
- **Real hardware moves.** A robot tool called with `--execute` can move real equipment. Keep the area clear and keep the emergency stop within reach. The robot's rules tell the agent not to move the robot unless you ask for that motion, but only your approval of each command and the robot's own stop controls keep it from moving.

______________________________________________________________________

## 6. Give the Agent the Documentation

- Inside the workspace, `sodero-help` prints every guide and `/opt/sodero/docs/examples` holds runnable examples. The robot's `AGENTS.md` points the agent to them.
- This documentation is also published in a form made for language models: `llms.txt` (an index) and `llms-full.txt` (all pages in one file) at the root of each documentation version, for example `https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/latest/llms-full.txt`.

# Create Custom Modules

A module is your own program packaged to run on the Station as a node, next to the built-in gateways and controllers. This page describes the package and how to build and install one from the [SSH workspace](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/ssh_workspace/overview/index.md). To install a finished package from your PC and manage installed modules, see [Modules](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/station/modules/index.md).

______________________________________________________________________

## 1. Package Format

A module package is a gzip-compressed tar archive with a `package.yaml` at its root:

```
my-module-1.0.0.tar.gz
├── package.yaml      # name, version, entry point, parameters
├── subsystem.yaml    # the node: its role and the ports it requires and provides
├── run.py            # your program (any executable)
└── ...               # your other files
```

| File             | Purpose                                                                                                                                         |
| ---------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `package.yaml`   | The module's name (for example `customer.patrol`), version, the command that starts it and its parameters                                       |
| `subsystem.yaml` | The node the module creates: its role (`gateway`, `component`, `compound` or `app`) and its ports with their contracts                          |
| `run.py`         | Your program. It implements the node's lifecycle (initialize, start, stop) with the Station SDK and serves or calls the interfaces of its ports |

Limits: 64 MiB per package (128 MiB unpacked).

**Complete guide and examples.** The SSH workspace of Stellar X contains the full package guide and runnable examples, including a status module, a navigation-goal client and a custom input gateway. Run `sodero-help packages` and see `/opt/sodero/docs/examples/` ([SSH Workspace](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/ssh_workspace/overview/index.md)).

______________________________________________________________________

## 2. Build and Install from the SSH Workspace

The Station SDK is not installed in the SSH workspace. Import it only in the code that runs on the Station, and give your program an offline `--self-test` to check it in the workspace, as the example does.

```
mkdir -p /workspace/my-work
cp -R /opt/sodero/docs/examples/native-status /workspace/my-work/
cd /workspace/my-work/native-status
python3 run.py --self-test                     # offline check
chmod +x run.py
tar -czf ../status-module.tar.gz package.yaml subsystem.yaml run.py README.md
sodero packages upload ../status-module.tar.gz --execute
```

Then add its node on the Station page ([Modules › Add and Start the Module's Node](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/station/modules/#add-and-start-the-modules-node)), or with `sodero topology add-node --kind package --package NAME --if-version N --execute`, and start it. `NAME` is the `name` in `package.yaml`; `N` is the graph version that `sodero topology get` returns ([sodero CLI](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/ssh_workspace/sodero_cli/index.md)).

**Tip:** An AI coding agent can write, check, package and install a module for you through the SSH workspace. See [AI Coding Agents](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/ssh_workspace/ai_agents/index.md).

# Write Device Bridge Drivers

The [Device Bridge](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/gateways/device_bridge/index.md) runs on a small computer next to the sensors and serves their data to Stellar X. It connects any RGB-D camera, IMU or wheel board for which it has a driver: one Python class on the sensor computer. The drivers that come with the bridge, for Intel RealSense D400 cameras, the TurtleBot3 OpenCR board and simulated devices, are examples; write a driver of the same kind for your own device. Nothing on the controller is rebuilt or modified.

This page is for developers. To install the bridge and connect it to the Station, see [Device Bridge](https://docs.sodero.io/stellar-x/v2.0.0/gateways/device_bridge/index.md).

______________________________________________________________________

## 1. Driver Classes

A driver is one Python class for one piece of hardware. It subclasses `Device` and each capability the hardware has: `Camera`, `Imu` or `Wheels`. One class may provide several, as the OpenCR driver provides both `Imu` and `Wheels`. The interfaces are documented in `device_bridge/devices/base.py`, and `device_bridge/devices/simulated.py` is the smallest complete example.

| Class    | You implement                                                                                                                                                                                |
| -------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Device` | `open()`: connect, or raise an exception with a clear message. `close()`: stop and release the hardware; safe to call twice. `self.options` holds the device's configuration block.          |
| `Camera` | `camera_info()` returns `CameraInfo(width, height, fx, fy, cx, cy)` of the aligned output; `read_frame(timeout_s)` returns `RgbdFrame(rgb, depth_mm, capture_unix_ns)` or `None`             |
| `Imu`    | `read_imu()` returns `ImuSample(gyro, accel, orientation_xyzw, source_time_ns)`, or `None` when nothing is new                                                                               |
